Beyond Sliders: Mastering the Art of Diffusion-based Image Manipulation\nL34: Yufei Tang Affiliation: FUYAO University Of Science And Technology Affiliation:  786650170@qq.com    Daiheng Gao Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Affiliation: samuel.gao023@gmail.com    Pingyu Wu Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Affiliation: Anhui Province Key Laboratory of Digital Security Affiliation: samuel.gao023@gmail.com    Wenbo Zhou Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Affiliation: Anhui Province Key Laboratory of Digital Security Affiliation: samuel.gao023@gmail.com    Bang Zhang Affiliation: Alibaba TongYi Lab    Weiming Zhang Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Affiliation: Anhui Province Key Laboratory of Digital Security Affiliation: samuel.gao023@gmail.com\nL35: ###### Abstract\nL36: In the realm of image generation, the quest for realism and customization has never been more pressing. While existing methods like concept sliders have made strides, they often falter when it comes to non-AIGC images, particularly images captured in real-world settings. To bridge this gap, we introduce Beyond Sliders, an innovative framework that integrates GANs and diffusion models to facilitate sophisticated image manipulation across diverse image categories.\nL37: Improved upon concept sliders, our method refines the image through fine-grained guidance—both textual and visual—in an adversarial manner, leading to a marked enhancement in image quality and realism. Extensive experimental validation confirms the robustness and versatility of Beyond Sliders across a spectrum of applications.\nL38: ###### Index Terms:\nL39: \nL40: image control, diffusion model, GAN, Perceptual loss\nL41: ## I Introduction\nL42: \nL43: In the field of image generation, the ability to control and edit images is crucial. One pioneering approach to image editing has been through Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), as introduced in the seminal work by Goodfellow et al. [cite21†1 ]. Since then, GANs have been extensively utilized for a multitude of image generation and editing tasks.\nL44: However, GANs have encountered certain limitations, notably in the precision of image control. This challenge has spurred researchers and practitioners to devise innovative methods to enhance control over image creation. Among these advancements, the StyleGAN series [cite22†2 , cite23†3 , cite24†4 ] stands out as particularly renowned.\nL45: With the advent of diffusion models, generative modeling has opened new frontiers[cite25†5 ]. Particularly, diffusion models using latent space have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in generating high-quality images. Unlike GANs, diffusion models gradually transform random noise into coherent images through a series of denoising steps[cite26†6 ]. This iterative process not only produces realistic images but also showcases intricate details and textures[cite27†7 ].\nL46: As for image editing, current diffusion-based SOTA: Concept Sliders[cite28†8 , cite29†9 ] enable fine control over specific features, such as age, gender, thus becoming a powerful tool for personalized image generation and editing[cite23†3 , cite28†8 ], advancing the boundaries of image editing[cite30†10 ]. However, despite these advancements, unresolved issues remain when testing images of natural scenes.\nL47: Natural scene images, also known as in-the-wild images, captured in uncontrolled environments, typically contain various lighting conditions, backgrounds, and subject poses. Editing these images presents unique challenges due to their inherent diversity and complexity, and poor generalization performance hinders Concept Sliders from landing.\nL48: As shown in cite31†fig. 1 , we introduce Beyond Sliders, which harnesses the power of GANs and diffusion models to achieve elaborative image manipulation on images of various types. Specifically, by utilizing Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)[cite32†11 ] within the stable diffusion framework[cite33†12 ], our method optimizes the generated images by innovatively combining a discriminator network and perceptual loss[cite34†13 ].\nL49: This approach ensures excellent image quality and realism, even when applied to complex and diverse natural scene images.\nL50: Overall, Beyond Sliders addresses the limitations of previous techniques, such as Concept Sliders, which struggle with the diversity and complexity of in-the-wild images. The adoption of conceptual triplet loss is also a key element in our work, which ensures the low-rank directions in diffusion latent space for targeted concept control.\nL51: cite35†Image: Refer to caption Fig. 1: Beyond Sliders evolved upon its precedant, Concept Sliders, in terms of identity-consistency and high-fidelity. cite36†Image: Refer to caption Fig. 2: Beyond Slider’s Workflow, utilizing a frozen SD and LoRA adapters to process image inputs. The model is optimized through perceptual loss, adversarial loss, and triplet loss to improve the generated outputs. Text inputs like ”Bald” and ”Bushy” guide the model to generate images with specific attributes.\nL52: Additionally, weight updates are performed using LoRA, allowing for precise control over both the quality and attributes of the generated images.\nL53: ## II Related Works\nL54: \nL55: Conditional image editing is gaining popularity, focusing on creating or adjusting images based on certain conditions. While GANs have been considered, we prioritize diffusion-based methods for their reliable and high-quality results.\nL56: Reversion[cite37†14 ] innovatively extracts abstract concepts from a few images, simplifying the process of concept-based editing with diffusion models. Concept Sliders[cite28†8 ], which employs LoRA[cite32†11 ] for precise control in diffusion models, represents a cutting-edge approach and seminal work in conditional image editing topic. By fine-tuning low-rank adapters, it allows for precise control over image attributes with minimal interference.\nL57: Notable developments based on Concept Sliders include TexSliders[cite38†15 ], which adds detailed texture editing, and SOEDiff[cite39†16 ], which enhances small object inpainting with advanced techniques. SCoFT[cite40†17 ] ensures diverse image generation through self-contrastive fine-tuning. These methods reflect the ongoing progress towards more intuitive and manageable image editing tools.\nL58: \nL59: By the way, our method fundamentally differs from existing latent space[cite41†18 ] manipulation techniques in several ways:\nL60: I. Integration of Triplet Loss: Unlike GANSpace[cite42†19 ] or linear SVM[cite43†20 ] approaches, our method incorporates conceptual triplet loss to explicitly align latent directions with target attributes, improving semantic control and precision.\nL61: II. Focus on Generalization: While prior methods like StyleFlow[cite44†21 ] often rely on specific attribute classifiers, Beyond Sliders leverages low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and adversarial training to generalize across diverse image types, including in-the-wild images.\nL62: \nL63: III. Diffusion Models: Existing methods are typically limited to GAN frameworks. Our work integrates diffusion models, leveraging their iterative refinement process for enhanced realism and flexibility.\nL64: IV. Perceptual Loss and Adversarial Training: Our method leverages perceptual loss and adversarial training to enhance image quality and semantic alignment. Perceptual loss captures realism through feature-level differences, while adversarial training teaches the model to learn complex distributions, overcoming issues like mode collapse and unnatural artifacts.\nL65: Together, they enable Beyond Sliders to balance semantic fidelity with realism, facilitating complex tasks like attribute disentangling and editing real-world images.\nL66: ## III Method\nL67: \nL68: As shown in cite45†fig. 2 , we utilized Stable Diffusion XL[cite28†8 ] as our base model, enhanced by LoRA[cite32†11 ], perceptual loss[cite34†13 ] and GAN[cite46†22 ] to improve the realism and consistency of generated images. The model consists of a generator (SDXL + LoRA) and a discriminator, trained together in an adversarial manner to ensure high-quality image generation.\nL69: ### III-A Preliminaries\nL70: \nL71: Diffusion Models Diffusion models are a class of generative models that operate by reversing a diffusion process to generate data. Initially, the forward diffusion process gradually adds noise to the data, transitioning it from an organized state $x_{0}$ to a complete Gaussian noise state $x_{T}$. At any timestep $t$, the noised image is modeled as:\nL72: \nL73:  | $$x_{t}\\leftarrow\\sqrt{1-\\beta_{t}}x_{0}+\\sqrt{\\beta_{t}}\\epsilon$$  |  | (1)\nL74: where $\\epsilon$ is randomly sampled Gaussian noise with zero mean and unit variance. Diffusion models aim to reverse this diffusion process by sampling a random Gaussian noise $X_{T}$ and gradually denoising the image to generate an image $x_{0}$. The objective of the diffusion model is simplified to predicting the true noise $\\epsilon$ by minimizing the following loss function[cite25†5 , cite47†23 ]:\nL75: \nL76:  | $$\\nabla_{\\theta}\\|\\epsilon-\\epsilon_{\\theta}(x_{t},c,t)\\|^{2}$$  |  | (2)\nL77: where $\\epsilon_{\\theta}(x_{t},c,t)$is the noise predicted by the diffusion model at timestep $t$ conditioned on $c$. In our work, we use SDXL[cite33†12 , cite48†24 ], which improve efficiency by operating in a lower dimensional latent space $z$ of a pre-trained variational autoencoder (VAE)[cite49†25 ]. Finally, the latent vector $z_{0}$ is decoded through the VAE decoder to get the final image $x_{0}$.\nL78: LoRA Adaptors To further enhance control over image generation, we use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to fine-tune the model[cite32†11 ]. LoRA decomposes the weight update $\\Delta W$ of large-scale pre-trained models into low-rank matrices $A$ and $B$, significantly reducing the number of trainable parameters. The weight update is defined as:\nL79: \nL80:  | $$\\Delta W=A\\times B$$  |  | (3)\nL81: where $B\\in\\mathbb{R}^{d\\times r}$, $A\\in\\mathbb{R}^{r\\times k}$, and $r\\ll\\min(d,k)$. By freezing the original weights $W_{0}$ and only optimizing the smaller matrices $A$ and $B$, LoRA achieves massive reductions in trainable parameters. During inference, the final weight is represented as:\nL82: \nL83:  | $$W=W_{0}+\\alpha\\Delta W$$  |  | (4)\nL84: \nL85: Increasing $\\alpha$ during inference strengthens the edit without retraining the model.\nL86: ### III-B Triplet Loss with $c_{+}$, $c_{-}$, and $c_{t}$\nL87: In our method, we adjust the model’s generation control by leveraging a triplet loss[cite50†26 , cite51†27 , cite52†28 ] involving $c_{+}$ (positive conception, e.g. bushy, old), $c_{-}$ (negative conception, e.g. bald, young), and $c_{t}$ (neutral conception, e.g. hair, age), which enhances or suppresses specific attributes in the generated image. Given a target concept $c_{t}$ and model $\\theta$, we aim to find $\\theta^{*}$ that modifies the likelihood of attributes $c_{+}$ and $c_{-}$ in image $X$.\nL88: This increases the likelihood of $c_{+}$ and decreases the likelihood of $c_{-}$ conditioned on conception $c_{t}$.\nL89: We achieve this by the following update:\nL90: \nL91:  | $$P_{\\theta^{*}}(X|c_{t})\\leftarrow P_{\\theta}(X|c_{t})\\left(\\frac{P_{\\theta}(c_{+}|X)}{P_{\\theta}(c_{-}|X)}\\right)^{\\eta}$$  |  | (5)\nL92: \nL93: Where $P_{\\theta}(X|c_{t})$ represents the distribution generated by the original model when conditioned on $c_{t}$. Expanding $P(c_{+}|X)=\\frac{P(X|c_{+})P(c_{+})}{P(X)}$, we derive the log-probability gradient:\nL94:  | $$\\begin{split}\\nabla\\log P_{\\theta^{*}}(X|c_{t})+\\lambda(\\nabla\\log(P_{\\theta}(X|c_{+})-P_{\\theta}(X|c_{-}))\\end{split}$$  |  | (6)\nL95: \nL96: To further strengthen control over the generation process, we introduce perceptual loss into the triplet loss framework. This helps to preserve the similarity between the generated images and reference images at the feature level, providing additional supervision signals during training.\nL97: \nL98: The perceptual loss function is defined as:\nL99:  | $$L_{\\text{perp}}=\\frac{1}{N}\\sum_{i=1}^{N}\\|\\phi(G(X_{i}))-\\phi(X_{\\text{real},i})\\|^{2}$$  |  | (7)\nL100: \nL101: Where $\\phi(\\cdot)$ represents the feature extraction function from a pre-trained network (such as VGG [cite53†29 ]), $G(X_{i})$ is the generated image, and $X_{\\text{real},i}$ is the corresponding real image.\nL102: \nL103: The combined loss function is expressed as:\nL104: \nL105:  | $$L_{\\text{total}}=\\lambda_{\\text{triplet}}\\cdot L_{\\text{triplet}}+\\lambda_{\\text{perp}}\\cdot L_{\\text{perp}}$$  |  | (8)\nL106: We introduce a dynamic weight adjustment strategy. Early in training, the weight of the perceptual loss is large, while the weight of the triplet loss gradually increases as training progresses to ensure semantic consistency in the generated images. The weight adjustment strategy is as follows:\nL107: \nL108:  | $$\\lambda_{\\text{perp}}(t)=\\frac{1}{1+e^{k(t-t_{0})}}$$  |  | (9)\nL109:  | $$\\lambda_{\\text{triplet}}(t)=1-\\lambda_{\\text{perp}}(t)$$  |  | (10)\nL110: Where $t$ represents the training step, $t_{0}$ denotes the switching phase, and $k$ controls the speed of the transition. This dynamic adjustment strategy enables the model to generate high-quality images in the early stages of training, while ensuring semantic consistency in the later stages.\nL111: The optimization of the denoising prediction is performed at each timestep $t$, by adjusting the noise prediction $\\epsilon_{\\theta}(X,c_{t},t)$ to minimize the total loss function $\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{total}}$. Thus, the optimization of denoising prediction is essentially carried out under the framework of the total loss function:\nL112: \nL113:  | $$\\epsilon_{\\theta^{*}}(X,c_{t},t)\\leftarrow\\epsilon_{\\theta}(X,c_{t},t)+\\eta\\frac{\\partial\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{total}}}{\\partial\\epsilon_{\\theta}}$$  |  | (11)\nL114: By doing so, the model can gradually optimize the generated images to ensure that they possess good visual quality and meet the expected semantic goals.\nL115: ### III-C Adversarial Training\n",

The weight adjustment strategy is as follows:\nL107: \nL108:  | $$\\lambda_{\\text{perp}}(t)=\\frac{1}{1+e^{k(t-t_{0})}}$$  |  | (9)\nL109:  | $$\\lambda_{\\text{triplet}}(t)=1-\\lambda_{\\text{perp}}(t)$$  |  | (10)\nL110: Where $t$ represents the training step, $t_{0}$ denotes the switching phase, and $k$ controls the speed of the transition. This dynamic adjustment strategy enables the model to generate high-quality images in the early stages of training, while ensuring semantic consistency in the later stages.\nL111: The optimization of the denoising prediction is performed at each timestep $t$, by adjusting the noise prediction $\\epsilon_{\\theta}(X,c_{t},t)$ to minimize the total loss function $\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{total}}$. Thus, the optimization of denoising prediction is essentially carried out under the framework of the total loss function:\nL112: \nL113:  | $$\\epsilon_{\\theta^{*}}(X,c_{t},t)\\leftarrow\\epsilon_{\\theta}(X,c_{t},t)+\\eta\\frac{\\partial\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{total}}}{\\partial\\epsilon_{\\theta}}$$  |  | (11)\nL114: By doing so, the model can gradually optimize the generated images to ensure that they possess good visual quality and meet the expected semantic goals.\nL115: ### III-C Adversarial Training\nL116: To further enhance the realism and quality of generated images, we introduce adversarial training: a generator and a discriminator[cite54†30 , cite46†22 ]. The discriminator is a binary classifier used to distinguish between real images and generated images, with real images sourced from the LFW dataset[cite55†31 ], and the generator is the combination of SDXL + LoRA.\nL117: The generator is trained to produce images that ”fool” the discriminator, and the generated images are pitted against real images in the discriminator, resulting in adversarial loss and perceptual loss[cite34†13 , cite53†29 ]. These losses are fed back to optimize the weights of both the generator and the discriminator simultaneously, which provides additional supervisory signals and enhances the visual quality of the generated images, helping the model avoid mode collapse.\nL118: Adversarial training helps address the issue where models may lose detail or realism when focusing solely on semantic accuracy (e.g., measured by CLIP). With adversarial training, we can maintain the visual quality and semantic relevance of the generated images.\nL119: ## IV Experiments\nL120: \nL121: In this section, we conducted multiple experiments to assess the performance and efficacy of our approach. These include evaluations across text-based and real-world scenarios, studies on rectifying flawed image outputs, and composition trials.\nL122: cite56†Image: Refer to caption Fig. 3: We show the composition capability through progressively compose multiple sliders from left to right (Top row), and demonstrate beyond sliders is capable to steer highly abstract concepts: hand and indoor layout to be physically plausible (Bottom rows).\nL123: ### IV-A Text Guided & In-the-wild Testing\nL124: \nL125: In  cite57†fig. 4 , we noticed that our method is adept at: 1) altering identities across both low-level (Fat) and high-level (3D) abstractions, and 2) robustly generalizing to diverse real-world exemplar data, encompassing everything from actual celebrity photos to 3D characters sourced from video games.\nL126: As we observed, the generated images were more natural in appearance, without any noticeable flaws. The modifications made to the attributes were both clear and striking. This demonstrates that Beyond Sliders is not only proficient in maintaining the fine details and naturalness of images but also shows an enhanced ability to manage sophisticated attribute alterations effectively.\nL127: Additionally, we evaluated the generated images from both models using CLIP and LPIPS scores. The results show that the images generated by our model achieved higher CLIP scores and lower LPIPS scores, indicating that our model produces more realistic image edits and is closer to the original images. [cite58†32 , cite59†33 ]\nL128: cite60†Image: Refer to caption Fig. 4: Beyond sliders enable meticulous adjustment of specific image attributes during the generation process, while demonstrate strong generalization on in-the-wild data, including 3D game character, celebrity.\nL129: ### IV-B Slider Composability & Erroneous Correction\nL130: \nL131: To further illustrate the disentanglement capabilities of our sliders, we selected three specific sliders: ”chubby,” ”age,” and ”smiling,” for our composable experiments. The rationale behind choosing these sliders is that the visual changes they induce are both intuitive and easily discernible.\nL132: Throughout the experiment, we manipulated these sliders at varying degrees to incrementally alter the image generation outcomes. The process begins with the creation of a base image derived from the initial textual prompt. Subsequently, the ”chubby” slider was applied to the base image. Following this, the ”age” slider was introduced on top of the ”chubby” effect to produce an intermediate image. Lastly, the ”smiling” slider was superimposed onto the image, culminating in the final output.\nL133: As depicted in the top row of cite61†fig. 3 and left part of cite62†fig. 5 , the final image, when juxtaposed with the base image, clearly exhibits the cumulative effects of the three sliders applied.\nL134: In the bottom rows of cite61†fig. 3 , by leveraging sliders, our model is capable of rectifying unnatural or distorted elements within the image: bad hands and anomalistic room.\nL135: \nL136: As the slider scales are increased, the model progressively generates hands that are more accurate, realistic, and proportionally correct.\nL137: cite63†Image: Refer to caption Fig. 5: We showcases supplementary results from the slider composability tests, underscoring that the model’s efficacy is far from coincidental. As shown in the results cite64†table I , for text-guided image generation tasks across various weights, Beyond Sliders and Concept Sliders show notable differences:\nL153: \nL154: For slider ”muscular” and ”age”, Beyond Sliders shows a clear advantage in LPIPS, particularly in the age task, where Beyond Sliders achieves an LPIPS loss of 0.027 compared to 0.038 for Concept Sliders.\nL155: Specifically, with slider ”long hair”, Beyond Sliders achieved a CLIP score of 29.06 and an LPIPS loss of 0.026, compared to Concept Sliders’ 29.03 CLIP score and 0.041 LPIPS. This suggests that Beyond Sliders offers superior performance in preserving visual consistency during image edits.\nL158: TABLE II: Ablation Study on loss configs\nL159: Setup  | CLIP $\\uparrow$  | LPIPS $\\downarrow$\nL160: --- | --- | ---\nL161: Full set  | 34.89  | 0.557\nL162: w/o adv  | 32.19  | 0.586\nL163: w/o perp  | 34.43  | 0.644\nL164: w/o adv & perp  | 33.17  | 0.629\nL165: ### IV-D Ablation study\nL166: \nL167: Here, we ablate the two key parts of our method: (1) perceptual loss perp and (2) adversarial training adv.\nL168: \nL169: cite65†Image: Refer to caption Fig. 6: Ablation study on loss configs.\nL170: As shown in cite66†fig. 6 and cite67†table II , perceptual loss helps maintain fine-grained details and ensures that the generated images closely resemble the original reference in terms of visual features. On the other hand, adversarial training contributes to enhancing the overall realism and naturalness of the generated images by encouraging the model to produce outputs that can ”fool” a discriminator network.\nL171: This combination allows for the generation of images that are not only semantically accurate but also visually coherent and lifelike.\nL172: The results showed that removing different modules led to varying degrees of decline in image quality. This indicated that the full model achieved a high CLIP score, meaning the generated images had strong semantic alignment with the text descriptions, while the low LPIPS score demonstrated a high degree of visual similarity between the generated images and the reference images.\nL175: After removing adversarial training, the CLIP score dropped significantly to 32.2, and the LPIPS score increased to 0.586. When both the discriminator and perceptual loss modules were removed, the CLIP score decreased to 33.2, and the LPIPS score increased to 0.629, indicating the importance of both components in generating high-quality images.\nL176: ## V Limitation\nL177: \nL178: In this study, we primarily focus on the field of conditional image editing, especially methods based on diffusion models. However, there are still the following limitations:\nL179: 1.Lack of experiments on the latest Flow-Matching models: We have not yet conducted experiments on the latest Flow-Matching models (e.g., Flux ^{1}^{1} 1 https://blackforestlabs.ai/, Stable Diffusion 3 [cite68†34 ]). These models exhibit significant advantages in generation quality and efficiency. Future research should consider incorporating them into experiments to evaluate their performance in conditional image editing tasks.\n"

+## 7. Compression 必要理论与审计窄核实际闭合
+
+本人实际读取2509.11208v1原件paragraphs24–64、80–98、120–174及完整必要Assumptions1/2、Theorems1–6、Propositions1–4、Corollaries1/2和§3公式块；311274 bytes/SHA `cde6f6e1b304e882fb1c9079f5be786842579d743d7e74000b6dfa5121973683`与作者request实际一致。没有全篇证明审计、完整附件/figure像素、代码执行或复现。此处关闭必要普通读取门，不追写成日期/Evidence完成。
+
+保留窄P：顺序扰动影响预测分布、概率空间的共享参数branch混合、信息预算与answer/abstain选择的具体形成条件。O(log n)依赖harmonic coordinate stability/additive positional-logit等假设；RoPE/LayerNorm名称及有限拟合不证明任意Transformer满足。Theorem3仅在模型类包含tied-weight branch与概率平均head时闭合；Theorem4/6的零残差还需exchangeable target在可实现凸包内，不能借Jensen授任意训练模型Bayesian/MDL最优。JS证书只约束置换分布离散，不证预测truth或安全。
+
+EDFL实际链为expected KL≥mixture KL≥Bernoulli KL：目标预算下界必要，不是预算足够就保证目标可靠性的充分条件。Theorem5等号除Bernoulli I-projection外还需第一步Jensen gap为零；Corollary1用O(q)写leading lowerbound时遗漏固定Bernoulli entropy项，uniform版本的−log2不能默默代补原式。AppendixA的min(U,B)期望下界性质不直接适用于audit采用的对称clip(U,±6)，单个gold token logratio平均也不等已知P分布的真实期望KL。ISR1/B2T/RoH可作为作者planner，不能由该链授确定幻觉阈值或部署认证。
+
+实际审计范围为Gemma2-9B、528 heldout、六置换seeds、clip6；96.2% boundary alignment、near0 hallucination、24.1% abstention和80.5% accuracy-on-attempts属于不同作者指标，不反造共同分母/错误数。AppendixH宣称3059总项，但来源列2000+2000+1000+500+300+且未说明最终选取归并；support-string/no-support构造与最终hallucination predicate/分母不是同一定义。42% Hotpot多跳/76% answer string仅该构造性质；repository withheld不授可复现、oracle-free qlo或已核部署。保留有限顺序敏感/混合与信息约束机制，不采用普遍hallucination prevention、calibrated safety或scale law。精确重开只需修订的充分条件/等号与entropy说明、实际clip估计关系和审计predicate/selection/denominator原件，非全部证明/代码。

+<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S4.SS5" title="In 4 Experiment ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.5 </span>Analyzing Hyperparameters</span></a></li>

+<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
+    
+<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Randomized smoothing is a well-established method for achieving certified robustness against <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-adversarial perturbations. By incorporating a denoiser before the base classifier, pretrained classifiers can be seamlessly integrated into randomized smoothing without significant performance degradation. Among existing methods, Diffusion Denoised Smoothing—where a pretrained denoising diffusion model serves as the denoiser—has produced state-of-the-art results. However, we show that employing a denoising diffusion model introduces a covariate shift via misestimation of the added noise, ultimately degrading the smoothed classifier’s performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel adversarial objective function focused on the added noise of the denoising diffusion model. This approach is inspired by our understanding of the origin of the covariate shift. Our goal is to train the base classifier to ensure it is robust against the covariate shift introduced by the denoiser. Our method significantly improves certified accuracy across three standard classification benchmarks—MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet—achieving new state-of-the-art performance in <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-adversarial perturbations. Our implementation is publicly available at <a href="https://github.com/ahedayat/Robustifying-DDS-Against-Covariate-Shift" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">this GitHub repository</a></p>
+  
+</div>
+<div class="ltx_keywords">
+<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>
+Certified Robustness , Randomized Smoothing , Denoised Smoothing , Adversarial Robustness , Denoising Diffusion Models
+
+</div>
+<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>
+
+<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success across various tasks, including image classification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. [2022]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al. [2022]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. [2022]</a></cite>, object detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zong et al. [2023]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. [2023c]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al. [2023]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oksuz et al. [2023]</a></cite>, and semantic segmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. [2023a]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. [2023c]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al. [2023]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. [2023b]</a></cite>, often surpassing human performance. However, these models remain vulnerable to data that deviates from training data distribution. For instance, adding even imperceptible perturbations to a data can cause a well-trained classifier to misclassify it. Such perturbed inputs, known as adversarial examples <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Szegedy [2013]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biggio et al. [2013]</a></cite>, pose significant challenges for deploying neural networks in safety-critical applications.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The sensitivity of neural networks to input perturbations has made robustness a critical concern, leading to the development of various defense strategies. Among the most effective approaches is adversarial training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madry et al. [2017]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goodfellow et al. [2014]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. [2015]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ding et al. [2018]</a></cite>, which generates adversarial examples during training and incorporates them into the learning process. Another interesting approach involves exposing classifiers to specific attacks during training. While such methods can improve the model’s robustness to specific perturbation, they often lack generalizability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tramer &amp; Boneh [2019]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaufmann et al. [2019]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmidt et al. [2018]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rice et al. [2020]</a></cite> and they do not provide formal guarantees of robustness.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">One line of thought pursued by researchers in the field of robustness is finding a method that guarantees robustness and, in other words, provides a mathematical certification. A lot of work has been done in this field <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wong &amp; Kolter [2018]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. [2018a]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mirman et al. [2018]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weng et al. [2018]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sinha et al. [2017]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. [2019]</a></cite>, but many of these methods are not applicable to deep neural networks. One of the certified robustness methods applicable to deep neural networks is randomized smoothing. This approach provides a robustness certification by transforming a classifier into a smoothed classifier. By averaging a classifier’s prediction on Gaussian-perturbed inputs, randomized smoothing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al. [2019]</a></cite> transforms a base classifier into a certifiably robust smoothed classifier.</p>
+</div>
+<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2509.10913v1/pipeline.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/179;" width="476" height="179" alt="Refer to caption">
+<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Pipeline of our proposed method. We optimize the perturbation <math id="S1.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> to induce extreme covariate shift during denoising and utilize it to train the base classifier.
+</figcaption>
+</figure>
+<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">While randomized smoothing theoretically guarantees robustness of any classifier by transforming it into a smoothed classifier, in practice, we cannot use pretrained classifiers since they are not robust to Gaussian-perturbed data. To address this problem, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salman et al. [2020]</a></cite> introduced denoised smoothing, which leverages a denoiser to preprocess perturbed inputs before classification. By incorporating a denoiser, pretrained classifiers can be effectively used within the randomized smoothing paradigm.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">One of the denoisers that has achieved excellent results is the denoising diffusion model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al. [2020]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. [2020a]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. [2020b]</a></cite>, which aims to obtain denoised data through a backward process by iteratively denoising the data. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite> demonstrated that by utilizing these models in denoised smoothing, it is possible to achieve excellent results in certifiably robust <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-perturbation using a pre-trained classifier and a pre-trained denoised diffusion model.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">However, diffusion-based denoising can introduce a covariate shift when noise estimation errors cause the denoised outputs to deviate significantly from the original clean data distribution. In diffusion-denoised smoothing, this shift propagates into the base classifier’s input, potentially reducing the smoothed classifier’s certified accuracy. Hence, while pretrained classifiers are compatible with diffusion-denoised smoothing, failing to adapt them to this covariate shift results in degraded performance.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To address this issue, we propose a simple yet effective approach to enhance the base classifier’s robustness against covariate shift induced by noise misestimation in diffusion denoised smoothing. Specifically, we introduce a novel adversarial objective function designed around the added noise in denoising diffusion models. Using an adversarial procedure, like projected gradient descent, we identify the noise configuration that generate the largest covariate shift and most effectively confuse the classifier. These adversarial noise samples are then used to train the base classifier, improving its robustness to covariate shift and significantly enhancing the certified performance of the smoothed classifier.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contributions:</span></p>
+<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
+<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
+<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We identify a critical limitation in Diffusion Denoised Smoothing: denoising diffusion models trained with mean squared error (MSE) loss introduce a significant covariate shift due to misestimation of added noise.</p>
+</div></li>
+<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
+<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To address this issue, we propose a novel adversarial training framework that explicitly targets extreme covariate shift cases, improving classifier robustness under noise misestimation.</p>
+</div></li>
+<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
+<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our approach on three standard classification benchmarks—MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet—achieving new state-of-the-art results in certified accuracy and Average Certified Radius (ACR).</p>
+</div></li>
+</ul>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>
+
+<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Denoising Diffusion Models</h3>
+
+<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM)<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al. [2020]</a></cite> is one of the most well-known types of generative models, recognized for its ability to generate high-quality data through a diffusion-based process. DDPM constructs a Markovian chain <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\{x_{t}\right\}_{t=0}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\{x_{t}\right\}_{t=0}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> with transition probabilities defined as:</p>
+<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p\left(x_{t}\lvert x_{t-1}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(x_{t};\sqrt{1-\beta_{t}}x_{t-1},\sqrt{\beta_{t}}I\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msqrt><mi>I</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\left(x_{t}\lvert x_{t-1}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(x_{t};\sqrt{1-\beta_{t}}x_{t-1},\sqrt{\beta_{t}}I\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
+<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+<p id="S2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{t}\in\left(0,1\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{t}\in\left(0,1\right)</annotation></semantics></math> controls the amount of noise variance added at each step. Since DDPM follows a simple Gaussian Markov chain, if we define <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\alpha}_{t}=\prod_{t=1}^{t}\left(1-\beta_{t}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo rspace="0em">∏</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\alpha}_{t}=\prod_{t=1}^{t}\left(1-\beta_{t}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, we have:</p>
+<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p\left(x_{t}\lvert x_{0}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(x_{t};\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}x_{0},\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}I\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><msqrt><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></msqrt><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt><mi>I</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\left(x_{t}\lvert x_{0}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(x_{t};\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}x_{0},\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}I\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
+<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+</div>
+<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In other words, <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> can be expressed as:</p>
+<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}x_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\epsilon" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msqrt><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}x_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
+<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+<p id="S2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,I\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,I\right)</annotation></semantics></math> and it is independent of <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In the reverse process, <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is progressively denoised step by step using a learned variational Markov chain. This chain is modeled as:</p>
+<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p\left(x_{t-1}\lvert x_{t}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(x_{t-1};\mu_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right),\Sigma_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\left(x_{t-1}\lvert x_{t}\right)=\mathcal{N}\left(x_{t-1};\mu_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right),\Sigma_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
+<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+<p id="S2.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)</annotation></semantics></math> are parameterized by neural networks and learned during training. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al. [2020]</a></cite> propose setting <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)</annotation></semantics></math> as:</p>
+<table id="S2.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta_{t}}}\left(x_{t}-\frac{\beta_{t}}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta_{t}}}\left(x_{t}-\frac{\beta_{t}}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
+<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+<p id="S2.SS1.p3.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)</annotation></semantics></math> is a denoiser that predicts the noise added to the data at time step <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. In DDPM, the covariance matrix <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)</annotation></semantics></math> is simplified to <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{t}^{2}I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{t}^{2}I</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{t}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{t}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is a fixed variance at each time step <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math> is the identity matrix. This simplifies the learning process by assuming an isotropic Gaussian distribution for the noise.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To train this model, the following optimization problem must be solved:</p>
+<table id="S2.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\underset{\theta}{\min}\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}x_{0}\sim\mathcal{D}^{trian}\\

+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
+<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+<p id="S2.SS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,I\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,I\right)</annotation></semantics></math> represents the true noise added to the data, and <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)</annotation></semantics></math> is the model’s predicted noise. This objective minimizes the difference between the true noise and the predicted noise across time steps.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In the reverse process of DDPM, the following equation is used to denoise and reconstruct the data:</p>

+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Randomized Smoothing</h3>
+
+<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">One widely recognized method for achieving certified robustness in deep neural networks is randomized smoothing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al. [2019]</a></cite>. In randomized smoothing, a classifier is transformed into a "smoothed classifier," offering a robustness guarantee for the newly constructed model. Let <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}</annotation></semantics></math> represent a hard classifier that maps an input to its predicted class. The smoothed version of classifier <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is then defined as follows:</p>
+<table id="S2.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.E8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{f}(x)=\underset{c\in\mathcal{Y}}{\arg\max}\ \mathbb{P}\left[f\left(x+\delta\right)=c\right]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>max</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">c</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.700em">𝒴</mi></mrow></munder><mi>ℙ</mi><mrow><mo>[</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{f}(x)=\underset{c\in\mathcal{Y}}{\arg\max}\ \mathbb{P}\left[f\left(x+\delta\right)=c\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
+<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{array}[]{cc}where&amp;\delta\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma^{2}I\right)\end{array}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{array}[]{cc}where&amp;\delta\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma^{2}I\right)\end{array}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+<p id="S2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> controls robustness/accuracy tradeoff. The following theorem provides an <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> robustness certification for randomized smoothing.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
+<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al. [2019]</a></cite>)</span></h6>

+<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">to be the two most likely classes for <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> according to <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{f}</annotation></semantics></math> with probability <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{b}</annotation></semantics></math>. Then, we have that <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{f}\left(x^{\prime}\right)=a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{f}\left(x^{\prime}\right)=a</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="x^{{}^{\prime}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></msup></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{{}^{\prime}}</annotation></semantics></math> satisfying</span></p>
+<table id="S2.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|x^{\prime}-x\|_{2}\leq\frac{\sigma}{2}\left(\Phi^{-1}\left(p_{a}\right)-\Phi^{-1}\left(p_{b}\right)\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|x^{\prime}-x\|_{2}\leq\frac{\sigma}{2}\left(\Phi^{-1}\left(p_{a}\right)-\Phi^{-1}\left(p_{b}\right)\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
+<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi^{-1}\left(\cdot\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi^{-1}\left(\cdot\right)</annotation></semantics></math> is inverse CDF of standard normal.</span></p>
+</div>
+</div>
+<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although randomized smoothing offers a robustness certification for the smoothed classifier, in practice, the performance of the smoothed classifier tends to be poor because the base classifier is not inherently robust to Gaussian perturbations. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al. [2019]</a></cite> address this challenge by training the base classifier with Gaussian data augmentation, improving its robustness to Gaussian perturbations. However, in SmoothAdv <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salman et al. [2019]</a></cite>, it is demonstrated that adversarial training of the base classifier using adversarial examples generated from the smoothed classifier within an <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-ball leads to better performance. SmoothMix <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeong et al. [2021]</a></cite> introduces a method where an adversarial example is generated from a clean input, and an auxiliary loss is computed using mix-up augmentation between the clean and adversarial examples. It then trains the base classifier using both the auxiliary loss and the Gaussian augmentation loss.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">MACER <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhai et al. [2020]</a></cite> takes a different approach by directly training the smoothed classifier rather than the base classifier. Its training process focuses on maximizing the certified robustness radius of the smoothed classifier. Alternatively, Consistency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeong &amp; Shin [2020]</a></cite> uses a distinct method by training the classifier to ensure that the smoothed classifier produces stable outputs within a local neighborhood, while also ensuring that the output remains as far from a uniform distribution as possible.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Denoised Smoothing</h3>
+
+<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although randomized smoothing offers robustness certification for the smoothed version of any classifier, in practice,it requires training the base classifier on noisy/adversarial examples, making it impractical to use a pre-trained classifier. Denoised Smoothing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salman et al. [2020]</a></cite> addresses this challenge by incorporating a denoiser before the base classifier, allowing for the use of pre-trained classifiers while still benefiting from randomized smoothing. Let <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}</annotation></semantics></math> be a classifier and <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> be a denoiser. The denoised smoothed version of the classifier <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as follows:</p>
+<table id="S2.E12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.E12.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="g(x)=\underset{c\in\mathcal{Y}}{\arg\max}\ \mathbb{P}\left[f\left(D\left(x+\delta\right)\right)=c\right]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>max</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">c</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.700em">𝒴</mi></mrow></munder><mi>ℙ</mi><mrow><mo>[</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>D</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(x)=\underset{c\in\mathcal{Y}}{\arg\max}\ \mathbb{P}\left[f\left(D\left(x+\delta\right)\right)=c\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
+<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+<table id="S2.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{array}[]{cc}where&amp;\delta\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma^{2}I\right)\end{array}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{array}[]{cc}where&amp;\delta\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma^{2}I\right)\end{array}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+</div>
+<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">It can be easily demonstrated that the robustness certification remains valid for denoised smoothed classifiers as well. The denoiser in denoised smoothing can be trained using Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss, stability loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salman et al. [2020]</a></cite>, or a combination of both. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salman et al. [2020]</a></cite> demonstrate that training with stability loss leads to better results.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Although a pretrained classifier can be utilized in the denoised smoothing approach, training the denoiser remains essential.
+To address this issue, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite> propose Diffusion Denoised Smoothing. In this approach, the noisy input is denoised using a denoising diffusion model at a specific time step <math id="S2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math>, determined as:</p>
+<table id="S2.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_left"><math id="S2.E13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}=\underset{t}{\arg\min}\ {\left|\sigma-\sqrt{\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\right|}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>min</mi></mrow><mo mathsize="0.700em">𝑡</mo></munder><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mfrac></msqrt></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}=\underset{t}{\arg\min}\ {\left|\sigma-\sqrt{\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\right|}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td>
+<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+</div>
+<div id="S2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This formulation selects the optimal time step <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> where the diffusion noise level best matches the target noise parameter <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t^{\ast}}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t^{\ast}}}(x+\delta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msqrt><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></msub></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t^{\ast}}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t^{\ast}}}(x+\delta)</annotation></semantics></math>. Since the denoising process in denoising diffusion models is iterative, it has a computational complexity of <math id="S2.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(t^{\ast})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(t^{\ast})</annotation></semantics></math>. This not only slows down the denoising process but also causes error accumulation over multiple steps, leading to a substantial discrepancy between the denoised image and its corresponding clean image. To address this challenge, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite> propose the use of a single-shot denoiser:</p>
+<table id="S2.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+
+<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padleft"></td>

A total of 3,000 samples were randomly selected from the CIFAR-10 dataset. For each sample, the noisy-then-denoised counterpart was computed using the time formulation described in Equation (<a href="#S2.E13" title="In 2.3 Denoised Smoothing ‣ 2 Background ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>).
