+<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>
+
+<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite> assert that Diffusion Denoised Smoothing is versatile, allowing the use of any pre-trained classifier. However, our observations in section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Covariate Shift Issue in Single-Shot Denoiser ‣ 3 Method ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, reveal a challenge with single-shot denoisers that may degrade the smoothed classifier performance. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel adversarial objective function to train the base classifier, as discussed in section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Dealing with Covariate Shift ‣ 3 Method ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>.</p>
+</div>
+<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Covariate Shift Issue in Single-Shot Denoiser</h3>
+
+<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The single-shot denoiser in eq.<a href="#S2.E14" title="In 2.3 Denoised Smoothing ‣ 2 Background ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> is a key component of Diffusion Denoised Smoothing, allowing it to integrate with any pre-trained base classifier. The effectiveness of this component plays an important role in the smoothed classifier performance. To evaluate the efficacy of the single-shot denoiser, we conducted an experiment on a randomly selected subset of 3000 CIFAR-10 samples. In our experiment, every sample is corrupted with Gaussian noise of a specified standard deviation and subsequently denoised using the single-shot denoiser at time <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math>, as derived from equation (<a href="#S2.E13" title="In 2.3 Denoised Smoothing ‣ 2 Background ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>). The noisy-then-denoised sample is denoted by <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="X_{0\lvert t^{\ast}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>t</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{0\lvert t^{\ast}}</annotation></semantics></math>. The efficiency of the single-shot denoiser is measured by calculating the distance between the clean and the noisy-then-denoised sample. The <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and LPIPS<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
+              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
+              
+              
+              
+            Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity</span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. [2018b]</a></cite> distances are chosen to evaluate geometric and perceptual similarity, respectively. Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.3 Denoised Smoothing ‣ 2 Background ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and LPIPS distances across varying <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> levels, illustrating a clear increase in distances between clean and noisy-then-denoised data as <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> grows. Significant geometric distances indicate that the noisy data is mapped to a point far from the clean data, potentially outside the base classifier’s decision boundary around the clean data. This can result in changes to the base classifier’s predictions, thereby degrading its performance and, ultimately, the performance of the smoothed classifier. Significant perceptual distances further support this observation.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">How can this covariate shift mathematically be justified? For this purpose, we need to examine the denoising diffusion equations. In the forward path, the clean sample is corrupted by a Gaussian noise as follows:</p>

+</table>
+<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\epsilon}\left(x_{t},t\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\epsilon}\left(x_{t},t\right)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the denoiser’s estimate of the noise <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>. Now, By substituting <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> from equation (<a href="#S3.E15" title="In 3.1 Covariate Shift Issue in Single-Shot Denoiser ‣ 3 Method ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>), we have:</p>
+</div>

+</table>

+<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Let the mismatch term <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{t}\left(x_{t}\right)=\epsilon-\tilde{\epsilon}_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{t}\left(x_{t}\right)=\epsilon-\tilde{\epsilon}_{\theta}\left(x_{t},t\right)</annotation></semantics></math> quantify the discrepancy between actual noise and its predicted counterpart. then,</p>

+</table>
+<p id="S3.SS1.p5.2" class="ltx_p">Thus, the noisy-then-denoised sample (<math id="S3.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="x_{0\lvert t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{0\lvert t}</annotation></semantics></math>) represents the clean sample (<math id="S3.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>), augmented by mismatch term. Since <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{t}\left(x_{t}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{t}\left(x_{t}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> may be non-negligible, the resulting sample <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="x_{0\lvert t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{0\lvert t}</annotation></semantics></math> can lie far from the original distribution, causing the base classifier to operate on out-of-distribution inputs. As this distribution shift occurs in the input space of the base classifier, we refer to it as a <em id="S3.SS1.p5.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">covariate shift</em> issue.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Dealing with Covariate Shift</h3>
+
+<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite> draw inspiration from denoised smoothing to develop diffusion denoised smoothing. By incorporating a denoiser before the classifier, denoised smoothing allows randomized smoothing to be effectively applied to any pretrained classifier. In denoised smoothing, the denoiser can be trained using either MSE loss, stability loss, or a combination of both. As discussed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salman et al. [2020]</a></cite>, the stability loss aligns the base classifier’s predictions on noisy-then-denoised data with its predictions on clean data. Superior results can be achieved by employing this loss exclusively during the training of the denoiser. Stability loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salman et al. [2020]</a></cite> strengthens the base classifier robustness against covariate shifts that may arise within the denoiser.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion Denoised Smoothing utilizes a single-shot denoiser derived from a denoising diffusion model. This model has been trained using MSE loss to effectively predict the added noise. Indeed, it appears that utilizing stability loss is more effective in enhancing the performance of diffusion denoised smoothing classifiers.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Thus, the observations in section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Covariate Shift Issue in Single-Shot Denoiser ‣ 3 Method ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> confirm the presence of covariate shift, and the preceding discussion highlights that employing a loss function like stability loss can be more effective. There are two approaches to address the covariate shift challenge. One approach to eliminate the covariate shift is to ensure that the input and output of the single-shot denoiser are closely aligned. To accomplish this, a diffusion model can be trained using a loss function such as mean squared error (MSE), enabling its corresponding single-shot denoiser accurately predicts the clean sample. By doing so, a denoising diffusion model can be transformed into a consistency model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. [2023]</a></cite>, effectively addressing covariate shift. But it is shown stability works better for training the denoiser. However, while stability loss has been shown to perform better for training the denoiser, training a denoising diffusion model with a new loss function remains computationally expensive and not always practical.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We propose an alternative approach that enhances the robustness of the base classifier to the covariate shift introduced by the single-shot denoiser, offering a significantly faster solution compared to training the single-shot denoiser. Since the covariate shift arises from the misestimation of added noise to the clean data, it is essential to ensure that the base classifier is robust to such misestimation. Therefore, the following optimization problem is proposed:</p>
+<table id="S3.E19" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
+

+</div>
+<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> represents the classifier parameters, and <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the Gaussian noise added during the forward pass of the denoising diffusion model. A significant challenge in this optimization problem lies in computing the supremum with respect to <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, which is inherently difficult. Rather than computing the supremum globally, we can instead identify the value of <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> that locally maximizes the loss. Thus, after sampling <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,I\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,I\right)</annotation></semantics></math> for each sample <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left(x,y\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(x,y\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, we iteratively update <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> using a procedure similar to projected gradient descent to maximize the classification loss:</p>

+

+</div>
+<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is updated over <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> steps, resulting in <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{M}</annotation></semantics></math> at the end of the process. This <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{M}</annotation></semantics></math> is then utilized to fine-tune the base classifier.
+This approach ensures that the base classifier becomes robust to <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> values that induce strong covariate shifts capable of misleading the classifier.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Extreme Covariate Shifted Data Finding Algorithm</h3>
+
+<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In diffusion-denoised smoothing, perturbed data are denoised using a single-shot denoiser derived from a pretrained denoising diffusion model. However, the output of the single-shot denoiser may deviate significantly from the clean data, particularly under larger perturbations. We refer to this issue as covariate shift, arising from the misestimation of the added noise.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To enhance the performance of diffusion-denoised smoothing, we propose identifying instances with extreme covariate shift and training the base classifier on them. Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.4 Distinction from Existing Approaches ‣ 3 Method ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> outlines the procedure for identifying these extreme cases. In this algorithm, the initial noise <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)</annotation></semantics></math> is randomly sampled and subsequently updated over M steps. At each step, the data are perturbed using the noise from the previous step, <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{m-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{m-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, and then denoised with the single-shot denoiser. The denoised data are then passed through the base classifier, and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> is updated by ascending the gradient of the classification loss to maximize the loss. Finally, the data are perturbed using <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{M}</annotation></semantics></math>, denoised with the single-shot denoiser, and incorporated into the training of the base classifier. Figures <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and <a href="#A2.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> illustrate the data obtained from this algorithm for different step sizes, with <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=10</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Distinction from Existing Approaches</h3>
+
+<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite> describe the covariate shift introduced by single-shot denoisers as ’hallucination after denoising’ and improve the performance of diffusion-denoised smoothing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite> by training the base classifier on data augmented with such covariate shifts. In other words, they address the following optimization problem for the base classifier:</p>

+<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although exposing the base classifier to covariate shifts during training can enhance its robustness to some extent, it tends to perform poorly on more challenging cases. How can we justify that training the base classifier with covariate shift-augmented data improves the performance of diffusion-denoised smoothing?
+This approach builds upon the stability loss concept, with the key distinction that it uses the true class label instead of the classifier’s output as the predicted class.
+On the other hand, Applying Jensen’s inequality to the convex <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-\log\left(\cdot\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\log\left(\cdot\right)</annotation></semantics></math> function yields:</p>
+</div>

+\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,I\right)\end{subarray}}{\mathbb{E}}\left[-\log\left(f_{\theta}\left(x_{0\lvert t^{\ast}}\left(\epsilon\right)\right)\right)_{y}\right]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>≤</mo><munder accentunder="true"><mi>𝔼</mi><mtable displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">x</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">y</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.700em">∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.700em">𝒟</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">ϵ</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.700em">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn mathsize="0.700em">0</mn><mo mathsize="0.700em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">I</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></munder><mrow><mo>[</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>log</mi><msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>t</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}\left(x,y\right)\sim\mathcal{D}\\

+<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_left_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
+</table>
+<p id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The right-hand side of the inequality (<a href="#S3.E22" title="In 3.4 Distinction from Existing Approaches ‣ 3 Method ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>) represents the loss function in (<a href="#S3.E21" title="In 3.4 Distinction from Existing Approaches ‣ 3 Method ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>), while the left-hand side corresponds to the classification loss associated with Diffusion Denoised Smoothing. Thus, the loss function in (<a href="#S3.E21" title="In 3.4 Distinction from Existing Approaches ‣ 3 Method ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>) serves as an upper bound for the diffusion denoised smoothing loss function. By minimizing the loss in (<a href="#S3.E21" title="In 3.4 Distinction from Existing Approaches ‣ 3 Method ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>), we also minimize the diffusion denoised smoothing loss, ultimately enhancing the smoothed classifier’s performance.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S3.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">However, simply augmenting the training data with randomly sampled noisy-then-denoised inputs fails to address more extreme misestimations of noise. We argue that the classifier should be robust not only to typical covariate shifts but also to the most severe shifts that can arise. Therefore, we propose an adversarial training objective that focuses on these hard cases, ensuring that the classifier generalizes better to all noisy-then-denoised inputs. In our proposed method, we first identify the challenging data, and then the base classifier is trained to become robust on these data. By training the base classifier to perform well on challenging data with significant covariate shifts, we anticipate that it will achieve improved performance when exposed to various noisy-then-denoised inputs. By adopting this approach, our method significantly outperforms the standard covariate shift augmentation training procedure in diffusion-denoised smoothing.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+</section>
+<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiment</h2>
+
+<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Initially, we compare our approach with the method proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite> and demonstrate that enhancing the robustness of the base classifier to the covariate shift introduced by the denoiser significantly improves the <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-defenses of diffusion denoised smoothing. We conducted experiments on three standard classification datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For evaluation and comparison with prior approaches, we employed two common criteria:</p>
+<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
+<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
+<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Approximate certified test accuracy at different radii:</span> This criterion measures the proportion of data points that are correctly classified by the CERTIFY algorithm without abstaining and have a certified radius greater than r.</p>
+</div></li>
+<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
+<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Average Certified Radius (ACR):</span> This criterion represents the average certified radius returned by the CERTIFY algorithm for test data points that are correctly classified.</p>

+

+</table>
+<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{test}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{test}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the test dataset, <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="CR\left(f,\sigma,x\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">CR\left(f,\sigma,x\right)</annotation></semantics></math> represents the certified radius returned by the CERTIFY algorithm, and <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{f}\left(x\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{f}\left(x\right)</annotation></semantics></math> is the smoothed classifier corresponding to <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
+</div></li>
+</ul>
+<p id="S4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Approximate certified accuracy gauges performance at specific robustness thresholds, while ACR indicates the overall robustness across the entire test set. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al. [2019]</a></cite>, we use the same sampling and confidence parameters in the CERTIFY procedure for all models to ensure consistent comparisons.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MNIST Configuration.</span> For the MNIST dataset, we use a pretrained denoising diffusion model available on Hugging Face<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
+            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
+            
+            
+            
+          <a href="https://huggingface.co/1aurent/ddpm-mnist" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/1aurent/ddpm-mnist</a></span></span></span> as the denoiser and a LeNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">LeCun et al. [1998]</a></cite> model as the base classifier. For this dataset, we evaluate the performance with <math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=\left\{0.25,0.50,1.00\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0.25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.00</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=\left\{0.25,0.50,1.00\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CIFAR-10 Configuration.</span> For image denoising, we use the denoising diffusion model from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nichol &amp; Dhariwal [2021]</a></cite>, following the approach of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite>. To ensure a fair comparison between our method and previous approaches, we employ a ResNet-110 as the base classifier for all algorithms utilizing randomized smoothing for certified robustness. For this dataset, we evaluate the performance with <math id="S4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=\left\{0.25,0.50,1.00\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0.25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.00</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=\left\{0.25,0.50,1.00\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ImageNet Configuration.</span> We denoise ImageNet data with the 552M-parameters denoising diffusion model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dhariwal &amp; Nichol [2021]</a></cite>, and employ 87M-parameters BEiT-v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peng et al. [2022]</a></cite> base model using implementation from timm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wightman [2019]</a></cite>. For this dataset, we evaluate the performance with <math id="S4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=\left\{0.5,1.0\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=\left\{0.5,1.0\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.p6" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">For all datasets, we set <math id="S4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=1</annotation></semantics></math> unless stated otherwise. The step size is set to <math id="S4.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta=0.1</annotation></semantics></math> for MNIST and CIFAR-10, and <math id="S4.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta=0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta=0.05</annotation></semantics></math> for ImageNet.</p>
+</div>
+<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>CERTIFY and PREDICT Algorithms</h3>
+
+<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">By employing a base classifier that is robust to the covariate shift caused by the denoiser, we utilize the same certification and prediction algorithms as in diffusion denoised smoothing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite>. In both algorithms, the input data, which is made noisy using different Gaussian noise samples, is first denoised and then passed to the base classifier.
+In the PREDICT algorithm, a majority vote is taken from the obtained outputs. If the number of votes passes a binomial test, the majority vote is returned; otherwise, the algorithm outputs ’abstain’. In the CERTIFY algorithm, we ensure that the majority vote is robust if its proportion exceeds that of the second-highest vote by a specified margin. The CERTIFY algorithm not only provides the classification output but also returns the corresponding certified radius.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the certified accuracy and radii of our method and diffusion denoised smoothing on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet, we utilize the diffusion denoised smoothing implementation. For all datasets, the parameters are set as <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.001</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{0}=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{0}=100</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=10,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10,000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=10,000</annotation></semantics></math>. The CERTIFY algorithm is applied to 500 randomly selected samples from MNIST and CIFAR-10, and 100 randomly selected samples from ImageNet.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Results on MNIST</h3>
+
+<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this subsection, we examine the performance of our method on MNIST and compare it against existing smoothing-based approaches, emphasizing certified accuracy at various radii and the impact of covariate shift.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Randomized smoothing demonstrates strong performance at smaller radii; however, its efficacy significantly declines as the radius increases. To address this issue, methods such as SmoothAdv <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salman et al. [2019]</a></cite>, MACER <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhai et al. [2020]</a></cite>, SmoothMix <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeong et al. [2021]</a></cite>, and Consistency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeong &amp; Shin [2020]</a></cite> have been proposed, which aim to directly or indirectly train the smoothed classifier for improved performance on the classification task. By employing these approaches, these methods improve the certified accuracy of the smoothed classifier and reduce the accuracy degradation, compared to randomized smoothing, as the radius increases.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Another line of research focuses on denoised smoothing, which incorporates a denoiser before the base classifier in the smoothed classifier pipeline. By denoising the perturbed data, these methods enable the use of a pretrained classifier as the base classifier.When an effective denoiser, such as a denoising diffusion model, is employed within this framework, the denoised data closely approximates the clean data. However, any residual distance between the denoised data and the clean data can degrade the performance of the base classifier, thereby affecting the overall effectiveness of the smoothed classifier.</p>
+</div>
+<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
+<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Certified top-1 accuracy on MNIST for randomized smoothing and denoised smoothing-based methods. For randomized smoothing methods, the base classifier (LeNet) is trained according to the procedure outlined in each method. In denoised smoothing, a pretrained base classifier (LeNet) on MNIST is used, while the denoiser is trained. In diffusion denoised smoothing (DDS), we compare a pretrained base classifier with a base classifier fine-tuned on covariate-shift-augmented data. Our method fine-tunes the base classifier using the proposed adversarial objective function and employs the resulting classifier in diffusion-denoised smoothing. Each entry shows the certified accuracy, with the clean accuracy for the corresponding model in parentheses, using values reported in the respective papers.</figcaption>

+</figcaption>

+<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion denoised smoothing builds upon the denoised smoothing framework by utilizing a denoising diffusion model as the denoiser. As shown in table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Results on MNIST ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, This method exhibits poorer performance at smaller radii (<math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\leq 1.00" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>1.00</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\leq 1.00</annotation></semantics></math>) compared to denoiserless approaches, such as SmoothMix <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeong et al. [2021]</a></cite> and Consistency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeong &amp; Shin [2020]</a></cite>, which do not rely on a denoiser. The strong performance of denoiserless methods at smaller radii is understandable, as they train the smoothed classifier directly or indirectly. However, the robustness of denoiserless methods is lower, and their certified accuracy deteriorates much more rapidly compared to diffusion denoised smoothing. As discussed in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Single-Shot Denoiser Analysis ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>, the denoiser maps the perturbed input to a point close to the clean data distribution, on which the base classifier was originally trained. Thus, employing denoised smoothing-based methods becomes more effective at larger radii.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">However,
+at larger radii, noise misestimation by the diffusion model can introduce significant covariate shift, leading to a decline in the smoothed classifier’s performance. To address this, our proposed method leverages adversarial training on the most challenging misestimated noise scenarios, thereby aligning the smoothed classifier more effectively with the denoiser’s output distribution and improving certified accuracy. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Results on MNIST ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, for radii greater than 1.0, utilizing the base classifier trained with our proposed objective significantly improves certified accuracy, achieving state-of-the-art performance and specifically, at <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=1.25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=1.25</annotation></semantics></math>, our approach outperforms the best baseline by <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.2</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points, increasing certified accuracy from <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="89.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>89.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">89.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="92.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>92.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">92.0\%</annotation></semantics></math>. Table <a href="#A2.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> reports the certified accuracy of the smoothed classifier for various values of <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> used in our experiments. We observe that for <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, at radii larger than <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MNIST dataset. Our method improves the Average Certified Radius (ACR) over diffusion-denoised smoothing, achieving a state-of-the-art ACR of <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.886" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.886</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.886</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=1.0</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Results on MNIST ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> illustrates the certified accuracy of our proposed method as a function of the <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> perturbation radius for different values of <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> on the MNIST dataset. As <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> increases, our method demonstrates improved certified accuracy. This improvement can be attributed to greater noise misestimation at higher noise levels, where making the base classifier robust to such misestimation results in better certification performance.</p>
+</div>

+<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Results on CIFAR-10 ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates the certified accuracy of various methods on CIFAR-10 across different radii. At smaller radii (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\leq 0.50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>0.50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\leq 0.50</annotation></semantics></math>), denoiserless methods demonstrate superior performance. For instance, SmoothAdv <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salman et al. [2019]</a></cite> achieves state-of-the-art performance at radii less than <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.50</annotation></semantics></math>. This method leverages randomized smoothing while training the base classifier with adversarial data generated from the smoothed classifier. By doing so, this method effectively addresses the classification task for the smoothed classifier to some extent. As a result, it demonstrates better performance at smaller radii. However, as perturbations grow, denoiserless methods degrade more rapidly than diffusion denoised smoothing, indicating their limitations in handling larger perturbations.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although diffusion denoised smoothing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite> allows the use of any pretrained classifier, its performance at radii less than 1.00 is inferior compared to other methods. its certified accuracy is significantly lower than denoiserless methods at radii below <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.00" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.00</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.00</annotation></semantics></math>. Specifically, at <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=0.75</annotation></semantics></math>, it lags <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="21.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>21.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">21.3</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points behind the state-of-the-art, and at <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=1.00" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.00</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=1.00</annotation></semantics></math>, the gap remains <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16.6</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points. This is due to the covariate shift caused by the misestimation of the added perturbation during the denoising process. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite> address this issue by training the base classifier on covariate shift-augmented data. By doing so, they achieve state-of-the-art performance at a radius of 1.00; however, their certified accuracy is 3.1 percentage points lower than the state-of-the-art at a radius of 0.75.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned in section <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Distinction from Existing Approaches ‣ 3 Method ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>, while training the base classifier on covariate shift-augmented data can enhance the performance of diffusion denoised smoothing, it fails to make the classifier robust against extreme misestimations of noise. Thus, in our proposed method, we first identify these extreme cases and then train the base classifier on them to enhance its robustness against such scenarios. Table<a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Results on CIFAR-10 ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows that training the base classifier with our proposed adversarial objective improves certified accuracy by <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.7\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> at radii 0.75 and 1.00, respectively, achieving state-of-the-art performance at these radii. Table <a href="#A2.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows that applying our proposed method increases the Average Certified Radius (ACR) of diffusion denoised smoothing for <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.25</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.50</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=1.00" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.00</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=1.00</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Results on CIFAR-10 ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> compares the certified accuracy of our proposed method with denoised diffusion smoothing as a function of the <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> perturbation radius for various values of <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> on the CIFAR-10 dataset. As illustrated, improving the robustness of the base classifier against noise misestimation plays a crucial role in enhancing certified accuracy. Since our method explicitly trains the base classifier to be robust against the specific distribution of noise misestimation, it consistently outperforms the baseline approach that uses random noise for robustness.</p>
+</div>
+</section>

+<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To assess our method in a more challenging setting, we use ImageNet as a benchmark to compare it with diffusion denoised smoothing. Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.4 Results on ImageNet ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> compares the performance of our method with those of the two methods proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite>. As observed, training the base classifier with our proposed objective outperforms training with covariate shift-augmented data. This is because the single-shot denoiser is more prone to noise misestimation in high-dimensional data, leading to greater covariate shift. Therefore, it is preferable to enhance the robustness of the base classifier on extremely covariate-shifted data. Figure <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> presents examples of the extreme covariate-shifted data identified by our method. As observed, the covariate shift can become more pronounced.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">By training the base classifier with our proposed adversarial objective, we achieve state-of-the-art performance across all radii. Table <a href="#A2.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows that our method improves the state-of-the-art ACR, increasing it from <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.311" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.311</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.311</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.367" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.367</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.367</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> and from <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.113" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.113</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.113</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.212" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.212</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.212</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, demonstrating an overall improvement in robustness across the entire test set.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.4 Results on ImageNet ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, similar performance trends are observed on the high-dimensional ImageNet dataset. Our method consistently outperforms the baseline denoised diffusion smoothing approach across different noise levels, highlighting the advantage of explicitly training the base classifier to handle noise misestimation even in more complex and large-scale settings.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Analyzing Hyperparameters</h3>
+
+<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our proposed method introduces three hyperparameters: <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{adv}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{adv}</annotation></semantics></math>. Below, we analyze the impact of each hyperparameter and discuss how to select the optimal setting.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The parameter <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> represents the step size used in the optimization process. In each row of Figures <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and <a href="#A2.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, increasing the step size amplifies the covariate shift observed in the image. Therefore, this parameter should be chosen such that the induced covariate shift does not significantly alter the image content. Empirically, we find that setting <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta=0.1</annotation></semantics></math> yields favorable results.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The radius within which <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> is updated is controlled by <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{adv}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{adv}</annotation></semantics></math>. Our observations on the MNIST dataset (Table <a href="#A2.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) suggest that optimization performs best when the radius is unrestricted, i.e., setting <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{adv}=+\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{adv}=+\infty</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Another parameter in our method is <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, which represents the number of update steps for <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>. Figures <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and <a href="#A2.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> illustrate that increasing <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=10</annotation></semantics></math>—while keeping the step size constant—amplifies the covariate shift. Table <a href="#A2.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Visual Interpretation of Extreme Covariate Shifted Data ‣ Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows that increasing <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> reduces certified accuracy at small radii but improves it at larger radii. This occurs because training the base classifier with a larger <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> exposes it to more covariate-shifted data, enhancing its robustness to covariate shift. As the radius increases, the covariate shift also intensifies. Consequently, base classifiers trained with larger <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> exhibit greater robustness to covariate shift, leading to improved performance of the corresponding smoothed classifier at larger radii. Although increasing the number of update steps for <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> enhances the performance of the smoothed classifier at larger radii, it significantly increases training time. Therefore, we set <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=1</annotation></semantics></math> for experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed method.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+</section>
+<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>
+
+<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion Denoised Smoothing extends randomized smoothing by enabling the use of pretrained classifiers, demonstrating strong robustness at larger radii compared to denoiserless approaches. However, its performance is hindered by covariate shift caused by noise misestimation during the denoising. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al. [2022]</a></cite> handle this shift by augmenting training with covariate shift-affected data, but their approach fails to address extreme misestimations. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel adversarial training objective that explicitly identifies and trains on the most challenging covariate shift cases. Our method significantly improves certified accuracy and Average Certified Radius (ACR), achieving new state-of-the-art performance in diffusion denoised smoothing.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
