+    <title>From PowerSGD to PowerSGD+: Low-Rank Gradient Compression for Distributed Optimization with Convergence Guarantees</title>
+    <updated>2025-09-14T12:54:28Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11254v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11254v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Low-rank gradient compression methods, such as PowerSGD, have gained attention in communication-efficient distributed optimization. However, the convergence guarantees of PowerSGD remain unclear, particularly in stochastic settings. In this paper, we show that PowerSGD does not always converge to the optimal solution and provide a clear counterexample to support this finding. To address this, we introduce PowerSGD+, which periodically updates the projection subspace via singular value decomposition, ensuring that it remains aligned with the optimal subspace. We prove that PowerSGD+ converges under standard assumptions and validate its effectiveness through empirical evaluation on large language model tasks.</summary>

+    <title>ICR-RL: Deep Reinforcement Learning via In-Context Regression</title>
+    <updated>2026-07-06T06:45:46Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11259v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11259v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Recent advancements in machine learning have largely been driven by foundation models (FMs) trained on large, diverse datasets, enabling them to generalize effectively to new, related tasks. However, extending this paradigm to reinforcement learning (RL), where an agent interacts with an environment to select actions, remains a significant challenge. Most existing approaches train FMs directly on sets of control tasks, but developing diverse RL environments and scaling training across them can be costly and complex. In this study, we explore a simpler alternative approach based on a classical reduction from RL to regression. We demonstrate that a foundation model pre-trained for regression tasks, when used as an in-context regression (ICR) model, can be directly applied to RL problems. Building on this insight, we introduce a gradient-free method, ICR-RL, that requires no additional training and leverages an ICR foundation model to tackle RL tasks. We evaluate our approach by applying the ICR model with the recently proposed TabPFN, which is trained on a wide range of regression tasks. Experiments conducted on the Gymnasium classic-control benchmark indicate that ICR-RL can compete with commonly used methods, including DQN, PPO and TRPO. These results show that ICR foundation models can effectively solve RL tasks without fine-tuning, demonstrating their potential as a foundation for RL-oriented models.</summary>

+    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11287v1</id>
+    <title>Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models by Self-Injecting Hallucinations</title>
+    <updated>2025-09-14T14:26:53Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11287v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11287v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) suffer from serious hallucination problems, where the model-generated responses are inconsistent with the visual inputs. Existing hallucination mitigation methods are mainly based on preference alignment and require external human annotations or auxiliary models for preference data collection, which increase costs and limit sustainable improvement. To tackle these challenges, we propose Autonomous Preference Alignment via Self-Injection (APASI), a novel and generalizable method that mitigates hallucinations without external dependencies. APASI leverages the target LVLM to self-inject hallucinations into a generated response, creating a pair of responses with varying preference levels. During the self-injection process, the dis-preferred response is generated based on three key observations of hallucinations, ensuring it simulates real hallucination patterns. This fidelity offers an accurate learning signal for hallucination mitigation. Moreover, APASI incorporates an iterative alignment training strategy combined with curriculum learning to periodically update the preference data with increasing challenge, enabling stable and continuous enhancement of the LVLM. Extensive experiments across six benchmarks show that APASI not only effectively mitigates hallucinations for three baseline models but also achieves comparable or even superior performance to alignment-based methods with external dependency, thereby demonstrating its effectiveness and generalization capability. The code is available at https://github.com/davidluciolu/APASI.</summary>

+    <title>Holographic Transformers for Complex-Valued Signal Processing: Integrating Phase Interference into Self-Attention</title>
+    <updated>2025-10-30T03:42:04Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.19331v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.19331v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Complex-valued signals encode both amplitude and phase, yet most deep models treat attention as real-valued correlation, overlooking interference effects. We introduce the Holographic Transformer, a physics-inspired architecture that incorporates wave interference principles into self-attention. Holographic attention modulates interactions by relative phase and coherently superimposes values, ensuring consistency between amplitude and phase. A dual-headed decoder simultaneously reconstructs the input and predicts task outputs, preventing phase collapse when losses prioritize magnitude over phase. We demonstrate that holographic attention implements a discrete interference operator and maintains phase consistency under linear mixing. Experiments on PolSAR image classification and wireless channel prediction show strong performance, achieving high classification accuracy and F1 scores, low regression error, and increased robustness to phase perturbations. These results highlight that enforcing physical consistency in attention leads to generalizable improvements in complex-valued learning and provides a unified, physics-based framework for coherent signal modeling. The code is available at https://github.com/EonHao/Holographic-Transformers.</summary>

+    <title>Nav-R1: Reasoning and Navigation in Embodied Scenes</title>
+    <updated>2025-09-13T16:31:03Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10884v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.10884v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Embodied navigation requires agents to integrate perception, reasoning, and action for robust interaction in complex 3D environments. Existing approaches often suffer from incoherent and unstable reasoning traces that hinder generalization across diverse environments, and difficulty balancing long-horizon semantic reasoning with low-latency control for real-time navigation. To address these challenges, we propose Nav-R1, an embodied foundation model that unifies reasoning in embodied environments. We first construct Nav-CoT-110K, a large-scale dataset of step-by-step Chains-of-Thought (CoT) for embodied tasks, which enables cold-start initialization with structured reasoning. Building on this foundation, we design a GRPO-based reinforcement learning framework with three complementary rewards: format, understanding, and navigation, to improve structural adherence, semantic grounding, and path fidelity. Furthermore, we introduce a Fast-in-Slow reasoning paradigm, decoupling deliberate semantic reasoning from low-latency reactive control for efficient yet coherent navigation. Extensive evaluations on embodied AI benchmarks demonstrate that Nav-R1 consistently outperforms strong baselines, with over 8% average improvement in reasoning and navigation performance. Real-world deployment on a mobile robot further validates its robustness under limited onboard resources. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/Nav-R1. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/Nav-R1.</summary>

+    <title>Robustifying Diffusion-Denoised Smoothing Against Covariate Shift</title>
+    <updated>2025-09-13T17:27:37Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10913v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.10913v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Randomized smoothing is a well-established method for achieving certified robustness against l2-adversarial perturbations. By incorporating a denoiser before the base classifier, pretrained classifiers can be seamlessly integrated into randomized smoothing without significant performance degradation. Among existing methods, Diffusion Denoised Smoothing - where a pretrained denoising diffusion model serves as the denoiser - has produced state-of-the-art results. However, we show that employing a denoising diffusion model introduces a covariate shift via misestimation of the added noise, ultimately degrading the smoothed classifier's performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel adversarial objective function focused on the added noise of the denoising diffusion model. This approach is inspired by our understanding of the origin of the covariate shift. Our goal is to train the base classifier to ensure it is robust against the covariate shift introduced by the denoiser. Our method significantly improves certified accuracy across three standard classification benchmarks - MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet - achieving new state-of-the-art performance in l2-adversarial perturbations. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/ahedayat/Robustifying-DDS-Against-Covariate-Shift</summary>

+    <title>ToMA: Token Merge with Attention for Diffusion Models</title>
+    <updated>2025-11-30T17:46:06Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10918v3" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.10918v3" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Diffusion models excel in high-fidelity image generation but face scalability limits due to transformers' quadratic attention complexity. Plug-and-play token reduction methods like ToMeSD and ToFu reduce FLOPs by merging redundant tokens in generated images but rely on GPU-inefficient operations (e.g., sorting, scattered writes), introducing overheads that negate theoretical speedups when paired with optimized attention implementations (e.g., FlashAttention). To bridge this gap, we propose Token Merge with Attention (ToMA), an off-the-shelf method that redesigns token reduction for GPU-aligned efficiency, with three key contributions: 1) a reformulation of token merge as a submodular optimization problem to select diverse tokens; 2) merge/unmerge as an attention-like linear transformation via GPU-friendly matrix operations; and 3) exploiting latent locality and sequential redundancy (pattern reuse) to minimize overhead. ToMA reduces SDXL/Flux generation latency by 24%/23%, respectively (with DINO $Δ&lt; 0.07$), outperforming prior methods. This work bridges the gap between theoretical and practical efficiency for transformers in diffusion. Code available at https://github.com/WenboLuu/ToMA.</summary>

+    <updated>2025-09-13T17:35:17Z</updated>

+    <summary>Recent advances in Earth Observation have focused on large-scale foundation models. However, these models are computationally expensive, limiting their accessibility and reuse for downstream tasks. In this work, we investigate compact architectures as a practical pathway toward smaller general-purpose EO models. We propose a Metadata-aware Mixture-of-Experts Masked Autoencoder (MoE-MAE) with only 2.5M parameters. The model combines sparse expert routing with geo-temporal conditioning, incorporating imagery alongside latitude/longitude and seasonal/daily cyclic encodings. To further assess generalization, we evaluate on the EuroSAT-Landsat dataset, which lacks explicit metadata, and still observe competitive performance compared to models with hundreds of millions of parameters. These results suggest that compact, metadata-aware MoE-MAEs are an efficient and scalable step toward future EO foundation models.</summary>

+    <title>Data-Efficient Ensemble Weather Forecasting with Diffusion Models</title>
+    <updated>2025-09-14T02:22:16Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11047v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11047v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Although numerical weather forecasting methods have dominated the field, recent advances in deep learning methods, such as diffusion models, have shown promise in ensemble weather forecasting. However, such models are typically autoregressive and are thus computationally expensive. This is a challenge in climate science, where data can be limited, costly, or difficult to work with. In this work, we explore the impact of curated data selection on these autoregressive diffusion models. We evaluate several data sampling strategies and show that a simple time stratified sampling approach achieves performance similar to or better than full-data training. Notably, it outperforms the full-data model on certain metrics and performs only slightly worse on others while using only 20% of the training data. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of data-efficient diffusion training, especially for weather forecasting, and motivates future work on adaptive or model-aware sampling methods that go beyond random or purely temporal sampling.</summary>

+    <updated>2025-09-14T05:05:27Z</updated>

+    <summary>Generating high-quality 360° panoramic videos remains a significant challenge due to the fundamental differences between panoramic and traditional perspective-view projections. While perspective videos rely on a single viewpoint with a limited field of view, panoramic content requires rendering the full surrounding environment, making it difficult for standard video generation models to adapt. Existing solutions often introduce complex architectures or large-scale training, leading to inefficiency and suboptimal results. Motivated by the success of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) in style transfer tasks, we propose treating panoramic video generation as an adaptation problem from perspective views. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that LoRA can effectively model the transformation between these projections when its rank exceeds the degrees of freedom in the task. Our approach efficiently fine-tunes a pretrained video diffusion model using only approximately 1,000 videos while achieving high-quality panoramic generation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method maintains proper projection geometry and surpasses previous state-of-the-art approaches in visual quality, left-right consistency, and motion diversity.</summary>

+    <summary>Large Foundation Models (LFMs) have demonstrated significant advantages in civil engineering, but they primarily focus on textual and visual data, overlooking the rich semantic, spatial, and topological features in BIM (Building Information Modelling) models. +    <title>ICR-RL: Deep Reinforcement Learning via In-Context Regression</title>
+    <updated>2026-07-06T06:45:46Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11259v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

+    <summary>Recent advancements in machine learning have largely been driven by foundation models (FMs) trained on large, diverse datasets, enabling them to generalize effectively to new, related tasks. However, extending this paradigm to reinforcement learning (RL), where an agent interacts with an environment to select actions, remains a significant challenge. Most existing approaches train FMs directly on sets of control tasks, but developing diverse RL environments and scaling training across them can be costly and complex. In this study, we explore a simpler alternative approach based on a classical reduction from RL to regression. We demonstrate that a foundation model pre-trained for regression tasks, when used as an in-context regression (ICR) model, can be directly applied to RL problems. Building on this insight, we introduce a gradient-free method, ICR-RL, that requires no additional training and leverages an ICR foundation model to tackle RL tasks. We evaluate our approach by applying the ICR model with the recently proposed TabPFN, which is trained on a wide range of regression tasks. Experiments conducted on the Gymnasium classic-control benchmark indicate that ICR-RL can compete with commonly used methods, including DQN, PPO and TRPO. These results show that ICR foundation models can effectively solve RL tasks without fine-tuning, demonstrating their potential as a foundation for RL-oriented models.</summary>

+    <title>PINGS: Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fast Generative Sampling</title>
+    <updated>2025-09-14T14:22:33Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11284v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11284v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>We introduce PINGS (Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fast Generative Sampling), a framework that amortizes diffusion sampling by training a physics-informed network to approximate reverse-time probability-flow dynamics, reducing sampling to a single forward pass (NFE = 1). As a proof of concept, we learn a direct map from a 3D standard normal to a non-Gaussian Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). PINGS preserves the target's distributional structure (multi-bandwidth kernel $MMD^2 = 1.88 \times 10^{-2}$ with small errors in mean, covariance, skewness, and excess kurtosis) and achieves constant-time generation: $10^4$ samples in $16.54 \pm 0.56$ millisecond on an RTX 3090, versus 468-843 millisecond for DPM-Solver (10/20) and 960 millisecond for DDIM (50) under matched conditions. We also sanity-check the PINN/automatic-differentiation pipeline on a damped harmonic oscillator, obtaining MSEs down to $\mathcal{O}(10^{-5})$. Compared to fast but iterative ODE solvers and direct-map families (Flow, Rectified-Flow, Consistency), PINGS frames generative sampling as a PINN-style residual problem with endpoint anchoring, yielding a white-box, differentiable map with NFE = 1. These proof-of-concept results position PINGS as a promising route to fast, function-based generative sampling with potential extensions to scientific simulation (e.g., fast calorimetry).</summary>

+    <title>Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models by Self-Injecting Hallucinations</title>
+    <updated>2025-09-14T14:26:53Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11287v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11287v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) suffer from serious hallucination problems, where the model-generated responses are inconsistent with the visual inputs. Existing hallucination mitigation methods are mainly based on preference alignment and require external human annotations or auxiliary models for preference data collection, which increase costs and limit sustainable improvement. To tackle these challenges, we propose Autonomous Preference Alignment via Self-Injection (APASI), a novel and generalizable method that mitigates hallucinations without external dependencies. APASI leverages the target LVLM to self-inject hallucinations into a generated response, creating a pair of responses with varying preference levels. During the self-injection process, the dis-preferred response is generated based on three key observations of hallucinations, ensuring it simulates real hallucination patterns. This fidelity offers an accurate learning signal for hallucination mitigation. Moreover, APASI incorporates an iterative alignment training strategy combined with curriculum learning to periodically update the preference data with increasing challenge, enabling stable and continuous enhancement of the LVLM. Extensive experiments across six benchmarks show that APASI not only effectively mitigates hallucinations for three baseline models but also achieves comparable or even superior performance to alignment-based methods with external dependency, thereby demonstrating its effectiveness and generalization capability. The code is available at https://github.com/davidluciolu/APASI.</summary>

+    <updated>2025-09-16T06:25:53Z</updated>

+    <summary>Unaligned Scene Change Detection aims to detect scene changes between image pairs captured at different times without assuming viewpoint alignment. To handle viewpoint variations, current methods rely solely on 2D visual cues to establish cross-image correspondence to assist change detection. However, large viewpoint changes can alter visual observations, causing appearance-based matching to drift or fail. Additionally, supervision limited to 2D change masks from small-scale SCD datasets restricts the learning of generalizable multi-view knowledge, making it difficult to reliably identify visual overlaps and handle occlusions. Through extensive evaluation on the PSCD, ChangeSim, and PASLCD datasets, we demonstrate that our approach achieves superior and robust performance. Our code will be released at https://github.com/ZilingLiu/GeoSCD.</summary>

+    <updated>2025-09-13T16:57:32Z</updated>

+    <summary>Despite ASR technology being full-scale adopted by industry and for large portions of the population, ASR systems often have errors that require editors to post-edit text quality. While LLMs are powerful post-editing tools, baseline full rewrite models have inference inefficiencies because they often generate the same redundant text over and over again. Compact edit representations have existed but often lack the efficacy and context required for optimal accuracy. This paper introduces CEGER (Context-Enhanced Granular Edit Representation), a compact edit representation that was generated for highly accurate, efficient ASR post-editing. A separate expansion module deterministically reconstructs the corrected text based on the commands. Extensive experiments on the LibriSpeech dataset that were conducted, CEGER achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, achieving the lowest word error rate (WER) versus full rewrite and prior compact representations.</summary>

+    <title>Harmful Prompt Laundering: Jailbreaking LLMs with Abductive Styles and Symbolic Encoding</title>
+    <updated>2025-09-13T18:07:56Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10931v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.10931v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks, but their potential misuse for harmful purposes remains a significant concern. To strengthen defenses against such vulnerabilities, it is essential to investigate universal jailbreak attacks that exploit intrinsic weaknesses in the architecture and learning paradigms of LLMs. In response, we propose \textbf{H}armful \textbf{P}rompt \textbf{La}undering (HaPLa), a novel and broadly applicable jailbreaking technique that requires only black-box access to target models. HaPLa incorporates two primary strategies: 1) \textit{abductive framing}, which instructs LLMs to infer plausible intermediate steps toward harmful activities, rather than directly responding to explicit harmful queries; and 2) \textit{symbolic encoding}, a lightweight and flexible approach designed to obfuscate harmful content, given that current LLMs remain sensitive primarily to explicit harmful keywords. Experimental results show that HaPLa achieves over 95% attack success rate on GPT-series models and 70% across all targets. Further analysis with diverse symbolic encoding rules also reveals a fundamental challenge: it remains difficult to safely tune LLMs without significantly diminishing their helpfulness in responding to benign queries.</summary>

+    <summary>In-context learning (ICL) in Large Language Models (LLMs) has shown remarkable performance across various tasks without requiring fine-tuning. +    <title>An Interpretable Benchmark for Clickbait Detection and Tactic Attribution</title>

+    <summary>The proliferation of clickbait headlines poses significant challenges to the credibility of information and user trust in digital media. +    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across diverse tasks, yet their ability to perform structured symbolic planning remains limited, particularly in domains requiring formal representations like the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL). Our approach focuses on teaching models to rigorously reason about action applicability, state transitions, and plan validity using explicit logical inference steps. +    <summary>Artificial intelligence (AI) is anticipated to emerge as a pivotal enabler for the forthcoming sixth-generation (6G) wireless communication systems. +    <title>SmartSwap: Swap-Based Memory Optimization for LLM Training under Varying Operator Sequences</title>
+    <updated>2026-07-15T13:51:17Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11076v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11076v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>The increasing size of large language models (LLMs) has led to a surge in memory requirements during training, often exceeding the capacity of high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Swap-based memory optimization incurs neither accuracy loss nor additional end-to-end overhead when effectively overlapped, thus being an attractive solution. However, existing swap methods assume consistent operator sequences, which is impractical in Eager Mode, where operator sequences can vary during change.
+  We propose Chameleon, which redesigns the end-to-end process of swap-based memory optimization and is the first work to consider varying operator sequences in Eager Mode. Chameleon (i) introduces a lightweight online profiler to enable continuous profiling for monitoring operator sequences, (ii) generates effective swap policies with limited operator information, and (iii) optimizes the policy execution module for accurate policy application and better performance. Experimental results demonstrate that Chameleon reduces profiling overhead by 84.25%, enables training models up to 4x larger than hardware memory while adapting to changes in operator sequences, improves performance by up to 38.94% compared to recomputation or high-degree parallelism.</summary>

+    <title>Fluid Language Model Benchmarking</title>
+    <updated>2025-09-14T05:49:42Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11106v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11106v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Language model (LM) benchmarking faces several challenges: comprehensive evaluations are costly, benchmarks often fail to measure the intended capabilities, and evaluation quality can degrade due to labeling errors and benchmark saturation. Although various strategies have been proposed to mitigate these issues, they tend to address individual aspects in isolation, neglecting broader questions about overall evaluation quality. Here, we introduce Fluid Benchmarking, a new evaluation approach that advances LM benchmarking across multiple dimensions. Inspired by psychometrics, Fluid Benchmarking is based on the insight that the relative value of benchmark items depends on an LM's capability level, suggesting that evaluation should adapt to each LM. Methodologically, Fluid Benchmarking estimates an item response model based on existing LM evaluation results and uses the inferred quantities to select evaluation items dynamically, similar to computerized adaptive testing in education. In our experiments, we compare Fluid Benchmarking against the common practice of random item sampling as well as more sophisticated baselines, including alternative methods grounded in item response theory. We examine four dimensions -- efficiency, validity, variance, and saturation -- and find that Fluid Benchmarking achieves superior performance in all of them (e.g., higher validity and less variance on MMLU with fifty times fewer items). Our analysis shows that the two components of Fluid Benchmarking have distinct effects: item response theory, used to map performance into a latent ability space, increases validity, while dynamic item selection reduces variance. Overall, our results suggest that LM benchmarking can be substantially improved by moving beyond static evaluation.</summary>

+    <title>AQUA: Attention via QUery mAgnitudes for Memory and Compute Efficient Inference in LLMs</title>
+    <updated>2025-09-14T08:20:48Z</updated>

+    <summary>The quadratic complexity of the attention mechanism remains a fundamental barrier to scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to longer contexts, creating a critical bottleneck in both computation and memory. To address this, we introduce AQUA (Attention via QUery mAgnitudes) a novel and versatile approximation strategy that significantly reduces the cost of attention with a graceful performance trade-off. Our method operates in two phases: an efficient offline step where we compute a universal, language agnostic projection matrix via SVD on a calibration dataset, and an online inference step where we project query and key vectors and dynamically select a sparse subset of dimensions based on the query's magnitude. We further showcase the versatility of AQUA by demonstrating its ability to synergistically accelerate existing token eviction methods like H2O and to directly reduce KV-cache memory size. By offering a controllable knob to balance efficiency and accuracy, AQUA provides a practical and powerful tool for making large-scale LLM inference more accessible and sustainable.</summary>

+    <summary>Practitioners increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to evaluate generative AI outputs through "LLM-as-a-Judge" approaches. +    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11303v3</id>
+    <title>Ko-PIQA: A Korean Physical Commonsense Reasoning Dataset with Cultural Context</title>
+    <updated>2025-09-29T01:32:59Z</updated>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11303v3" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
+    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11303v3" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
+    <summary>Physical commonsense reasoning datasets like PIQA are predominantly English-centric and lack cultural diversity. We introduce Ko-PIQA, a Korean physical commonsense reasoning dataset that incorporates cultural context. Starting from 3.01 million web-crawled questions, we employed a multi-stage filtering approach using three language models to identify 11,553 PIQA-style questions. Through GPT-4o refinement and human validation, we obtained 441 high-quality question-answer pairs. A key feature of Ko-PIQA is its cultural grounding: 19.7% of questions contain culturally specific elements like traditional Korean foods (kimchi), clothing (hanbok), and specialized appliances (kimchi refrigerators) that require culturally-aware reasoning beyond direct translation. We evaluate seven language models on Ko-PIQA, with the best model achieving 83.22% accuracy while the weakest reaches only 59.86%, demonstrating significant room for improvement. Models particularly struggle with culturally specific scenarios, highlighting the importance of culturally diverse datasets. Ko-PIQA serves as both a benchmark for Korean language models and a foundation for more inclusive commonsense reasoning research. The dataset and code will be publicly available.</summary>

+    "title": "Free-MAD: Consensus-Free Multi-Agent Debate",
+    "summary": "Multi-agent debate (MAD) is an emerging approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Existing MAD methods rely on multiple rounds of interaction among agents to reach consensus, and the final output is selected by majority voting in the last round. However, this consensus-based design faces several limitations. First, multiple rounds of communication increases token overhead and limits scalability. Second, due to the inherent conformity of LLMs, agents that initially produce correct responses may be influenced by incorrect ones during the debate process, causing error propagation. Third, majority voting introduces randomness and unfairness in the decision-making phase, and can degrade the reasoning performance. To address these issues, we propose \\textsc{Free-MAD}, a novel MAD framework that eliminates the need for consensus among agents. \\textsc{Free-MAD} introduces a novel score-based decision mechanism that evaluates the entire debate trajectory rather than relying on the last round only. This mechanism tracks how each agent's reasoning evolves, enabling more accurate and fair outcomes. In addition, \\textsc{Free-MAD} reconstructs the debate phase by introducing anti-conformity, a mechanism that enables agents to mitigate excessive influence from the majority. Experiments on eight benchmark datasets demonstrate that \\textsc{Free-MAD} significantly improves reasoning performance while requiring only a single-round debate and thus reducing token costs. We also show that compared to existing MAD approaches, \\textsc{Free-MAD} exhibits improved robustness in real-world attack scenarios.",

+    "summary": "Language model (LM) benchmarking faces several challenges: comprehensive evaluations are costly, benchmarks often fail to measure the intended capabilities, and evaluation quality can degrade due to labeling errors and benchmark saturation. +"""Compare bounded Sep14 discovery fields with this day's prior abstracts."""
+import json
+from pathlib import Path
+import re
+import sys
+import xml.etree.ElementTree as E
+
+BASE = Path(__file__).parent
+NS = {"a": "http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom", "o": "http://a9.com/-/spec/opensearch/1.1/", "x": "http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"}
+
+
+def identity(url):
+    return re.search(r"\d{4}\.\d{4,5}", url).group()
+
+
+def normalize(value):
+    return " ".join((value or "").split())
+
+
+def load():
+    rows = {}
+    for theme in ("model", "systems", "agents", "multimodal"):
+        root = E.parse(BASE / ("SUP_arxiv-" + theme + "_20261012.raw")).getroot()
+        entries = root.findall("a:entry", NS)
+        print(theme, "total", root.findtext("o:totalResults", namespaces=NS), "returned", len(entries))
+        for entry in entries:
+            row = {field: normalize(entry.findtext("a:" + field, namespaces=NS)) for field in ("id", "title", "summary", "published", "updated")}
+            row["comment"] = normalize(entry.findtext("x:comment", namespaces=NS))
+            row["journal_ref"] = normalize(entry.findtext("x:journal_ref", namespaces=NS))
+            key = identity(row["id"])
+            if key not in rows:
+                rows[key] = row
+    old = {identity(r["id"]): r for r in json.loads((BASE / "scoped-abstracts.json").read_text())}
+    result = []
+    for key, row in sorted(rows.items()):
+        row["identity"] = key
+        prior = old.get(key)
+        row["prior_state"] = "new" if prior is None else "same" if all(normalize(prior.get(f)) == row[f] for f in ("id", "title", "summary")) else "changed"
+        row["prior_id"] = prior["id"] if prior else None
+        result.append(row)
+    return result
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    rows = load()
+    if sys.argv[1] == "save":
+        (BASE / "SUP_atoms_20261012.json").write_text(json.dumps(rows, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) + "\n")
+    else:
+        lo, hi = map(int, sys.argv[1].split("-"))
+        for i, row in enumerate(rows[lo:hi + 1], lo):
+            print(i, row["identity"], row["prior_state"], row["id"], "submitted", row["published"])
+            print(row["title"])
+            print(row["summary"])
+            print("comment:", row["comment"], "journal:", row["journal_ref"])

+"""Sep14 BJT bounded discovery captures; submitted is not public date."""
+import datetime
+import hashlib
+import json
+import pathlib
+import sys
+import urllib.error
+import urllib.parse
+import urllib.request
+
+BASE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent
+THEMES = {
+    "model": '(cat:cs.CL OR cat:cs.LG) AND (all:"language model" OR all:transformer OR all:"mixture of experts" OR all:"foundation model") AND (all:architecture OR all:attention OR all:optimization OR all:training OR all:"post-training")',
+    "systems": '(cat:cs.DC OR cat:cs.AR OR cat:cs.PL OR cat:cs.OS OR cat:cs.PF OR cat:cs.LG OR cat:cs.CL) AND (all:"language model" OR all:GPU OR all:LLM) AND (all:inference OR all:communication OR all:kernel OR all:serving OR all:parallel OR all:compiler)',
+    "agents": '(cat:cs.AI OR cat:cs.CL OR cat:cs.IR OR cat:cs.MA) AND (all:"language model" OR all:LLM) AND (all:agent OR all:retrieval OR all:memory OR all:safety OR all:jailbreak OR all:"tool calling")',
+    "multimodal": '(cat:cs.CV OR cat:cs.RO OR cat:cs.LG OR cat:cs.CL) AND (all:"foundation model" OR all:"world model" OR all:"vision language" OR all:"vision-language-action" OR all:"video generation" OR all:diffusion)',
+}
+URLS = {
+    "openai": "https://openai.com/news/rss.xml",
+    "anthropic": "https://www.anthropic.com/research",
+    "google-pubs": "https://research.google/pubs/",
+    "google-month": "https://research.google/blog/2025/09/",
+    "deepmind": "https://deepmind.google/research/",
+    "meta": "https://ai.meta.com/research/",
+    "qwen": "https://qwen.ai/api/page_config?code=research.research-list",
+    "deepseek": "https://api-docs.deepseek.com/updates/",
+    "moonshot": "https://platform.kimi.com/blog",
+    "hunyuan": "https://hunyuan.tencent.com/research",
+    "zai": "https://www.zhipuai.cn/zh/research",
+    "seed": "https://seed.bytedance.com/en/research",
+    "ernie": "https://ernie.baidu.com/blog/zh/",
+    "mimo": "https://mimo.xiaomi.com/",
+    "minimax-en": "https://www.minimax.io/blog",
+    "minimax-cn": "https://www.minimaxi.com/blog",
+}
+for name, theme in THEMES.items():
+    URLS["arxiv-" + name] = "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?" + urllib.parse.urlencode({
+        "search_query": theme + " AND submittedDate:[202509131600 TO 202509141559]",
+        "start": 0, "max_results": 150, "sortBy": "submittedDate", "sortOrder": "ascending",
+    })
+
+
+def capture(name, url):
+    record = {"url": url, "checked_utc": datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat(),
+              "purpose": "Sep14 full BJT natural day; discovery is not public-date evidence",
+              "method": "GET", "headers": {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"}}
+    data = None
+    if name.startswith("seed-"):
+        record["headers"]["x-tt-locale"] = "US"
+    if name.startswith("hunyuan-list"):
+        record.update(method="POST", body={"pageNum": 1, "pageSize": 1000, "renderType": 0})
+        record["headers"]["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
+        if name.startswith("hunyuan-list-zh"):
+            record["headers"]["accept-language"] = "zh"
+        data = json.dumps(record["body"]).encode()
+    try:
+        with urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, headers=record["headers"], data=data), timeout=45) as response:
+            body = response.read()
+            record.update(status=response.status, final_url=response.url)
+    except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
+        body = error.read()
+        record.update(status=error.code, error=str(error))
+    except Exception as error:
+        body = b""
+        record["error"] = str(error)
+    record.update(bytes=len(body), sha256=hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest())
+    (BASE / ("SUP_" + name + "_20261012.raw")).write_bytes(body)
+    (BASE / ("SUP_" + name + "_20261012.request.json")).write_text(json.dumps(record, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) + "\n")
+    print(name, record.get("status"), len(body), record.get("error", ""), flush=True)
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    if len(sys.argv) == 3 and sys.argv[2].startswith("https://"):
+        capture(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])
+    else:
+        for key in sys.argv[1:]:
+            capture(key, URLS[key])

+<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
+<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Predictable Compression Failures 
+<br class="ltx_break">Why Language Models Actually Hallucinate</h1>
+<div class="ltx_authors">
+<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
+<span class="ltx_personname">Leon Chlon
+</span></span>
+<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
+<span class="ltx_personname">Ahmed Karim
+</span></span>
+<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
+<span class="ltx_personname">Maggie Chlon
+</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
+<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hassana Labs</span>
+</span>
+<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{lc574@cantab.ac.uk}</span></a>
+</span></span></span></span></div>
+
+<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
+    
+<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models perform near-Bayesian inference yet violate permutation invariance on exchangeable data. We resolve this by showing transformers minimize <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">expected</span> conditional description length (cross-entropy) over orderings, <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\ell(Y\!\mid\!\Gamma_{\pi}(X))]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mpadded style="width:0.633em;" width="0.633em"><mi>Y</mi></mpadded><mpadded style="width:0.052em;" width="0.052em"><mo fence="true">∣</mo></mpadded><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\ell(Y\!\mid\!\Gamma_{\pi}(X))]</annotation></semantics></math>, which admits a Kolmogorov-complexity interpretation up to additive constants, rather than the permutation-invariant description length <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(Y\!\mid\!X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mpadded style="width:0.633em;" width="0.633em"><mi>Y</mi></mpadded><mpadded style="width:0.052em;" width="0.052em"><mo fence="true">∣</mo></mpadded><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(Y\!\mid\!X)</annotation></semantics></math>. This makes them <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bayesian in expectation, not in realization</span>. We derive (i) a <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Quantified Martingale Violation</span> bound showing order-induced deviations scale as <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\log n)</annotation></semantics></math> with constants; (ii) the <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Expectation-level Decompression Law</span> linking information budgets to reliability for Bernoulli predicates; and (iii) deployable planners (B2T/RoH/ISR) for answer/abstain decisions. Empirically, permutation dispersion follows <math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a+b\ln n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a+b\ln n</annotation></semantics></math> (Qwen2-7B <math id="abstract1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b\approx 0.377" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.377</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b\approx 0.377</annotation></semantics></math>, Llama-3.1-8B <math id="abstract1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b\approx 0.147" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.147</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b\approx 0.147</annotation></semantics></math>); permutation <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">mixtures</span> improve ground-truth likelihood/accuracy; and randomized <span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">dose-response</span> shows hallucinations drop by <math id="abstract1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>0.13 per additional nat. A pre-specified audit with a fixed ISR=1.0 achieves <span id="abstract1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">near-0% hallucinations</span> via calibrated refusal at <span id="abstract1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">24%</span> abstention. The framework turns hallucinations into predictable <span id="abstract1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">compression failures</span> and enables principled information budgeting.</p>
+  
+</div>
+<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>
+
+<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a fundamental paradox: they demonstrate remarkable in-context learning capabilities consistent with Bayesian inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al. [2022]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. [2023]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al. [2023]</a></cite>, yet systematically violate the permutation invariance that characterizes Bayesian predictive distributions on exchangeable data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Falck et al. [2024]</a></cite>. For truly exchangeable sequences where <math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=p(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(n)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=p(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(n)})</annotation></semantics></math>, Bayesian inference yields predictive distributions satisfying <math id="S1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1})|X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1})|X_{\pi(1)},\ldots,X_{\pi(n)}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1})|X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1})|X_{\pi(1)},\ldots,X_{\pi(n)}]</annotation></semantics></math> for any permutation <math id="S1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. The violation of this property indicates a mismatch between transformer architectures and exchangeability assumptions, yet transformers achieve near-optimal statistical performance across diverse tasks. How can models be simultaneously Bayesian and non-Bayesian?</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We validate theory using observables not defined by our metrics: ground-truth likelihood/accuracy under permutation mixtures, the log-scaling of permutation-induced dispersion, and randomized dose-response of hallucination to information budgets (see Appendix B for full non-circular validation principle).</p>
+</div>
+<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.1 </span>Our Contributions</h3>
+
+<div id="S1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We resolve this paradox through three interconnected theoretical and empirical contributions:</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1. Theoretical Resolution: Conditional Complexity Minimization.</span> We show that transformers with positional encodings minimize expected conditional description length (cross-entropy), <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\ell(Y|\Gamma_{\pi}(X))]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\ell(Y|\Gamma_{\pi}(X))]</annotation></semantics></math>, rather than the permutation-invariant <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(Y|X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(Y|X)</annotation></semantics></math>. This admits a Kolmogorov-complexity interpretation up to additive constants. This fundamental distinction explains why transformers are “Bayesian in expectation, not in realization”: they achieve entropy-level compression and calibration when averaged over orderings but systematically deviate for fixed input sequences. Our Quantified Martingale Violation theorem (Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Quantified Martingale Violation). ‣ 3.2 Quantified Martingale Violations ‣ 3 Theory: Order-Sensitive Information-Theoretic Guarantees ‣ Predictable Compression Failures Why Language Models Actually Hallucinate" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) provides an explicit <math id="S1.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\log n)</annotation></semantics></math> upper bound with constants for these deviations under harmonic positional decay.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2. Compression Failure Framework: From Theory to Hallucination.</span> Building on recent connections between compression and learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Delétang et al. [2023]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kalai and Vempala [2024]</a></cite>, we develop the Expectation-level Decompression Law (EDFL, Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem5" title="Theorem 5 (Expectation-level Decompression Law (EDFL)). ‣ 3.4 The Expectation-level Decompression Law ‣ 3 Theory: Order-Sensitive Information-Theoretic Guarantees ‣ Predictable Compression Failures Why Language Models Actually Hallucinate" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) that quantifies precisely how much information <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\Delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\Delta}</annotation></semantics></math> is required to lift an event’s probability from prior mass <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>q</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{q}</annotation></semantics></math> to posterior mass <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. Unlike existing work that treats compression as binary success/failure, EDFL provides exact bounds: for fixed <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=1-\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=1-\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, achieving reliability <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math> for rare events (<math id="S1.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\ll 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>≪</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q\ll 1</annotation></semantics></math>) requires <math id="S1.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\Delta}\geq(1-\varepsilon)\log\frac{1}{\bar{q}}+O(\bar{q})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mover accent="true"><mi>q</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>q</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\Delta}\geq(1-\varepsilon)\log\frac{1}{\bar{q}}+O(\bar{q})</annotation></semantics></math> nats. This transforms hallucination from an unpredictable failure mode into a quantifiable consequence of information insufficiency.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3. Operational Deployment Tools.</span> We bridge theory and practice through three metrics derived from EDFL:</p>
+<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
+<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
+<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bits-to-Trust (B2T)</span>: Information needed for target reliability <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math></p>
+</div></li>
+<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
+<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk-of-Hallucination (RoH)</span>: Achievable error given information budget</p>
+</div></li>
+<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
+<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Information Sufficiency Ratio (ISR)</span>: Ratio determining abstention decisions</p>
+</div></li>
+</ul>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">These planners align with the pre-specified ISR boundary in frontier model audits, enabling practitioners to predict hallucination risk before generation and manage it through information budgeting.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.2 </span>Empirical Validation</h3>
+
+<div id="S1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We validate our framework through three complementary experiments:</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Empirical (Primary, non-circular).</span>
+(i) Permutation mixtures improve ground-truth likelihood/accuracy (mixture Jensen gain).
+(ii) Permutation dispersion follows <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a+b\ln n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a+b\ln n</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b\approx 0.377" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.377</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b\approx 0.377</annotation></semantics></math> across 3,059 items.
+(iii) Randomized dose-response shows <math id="S1.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 0.13" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.13</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 0.13</annotation></semantics></math> fewer hallucinations per nat.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Deployment (Secondary, calibration only).</span>
+A pre-specified ISR boundary (<math id="S1.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=1.0</annotation></semantics></math>) exhibits 96.2% boundary alignment; this is reported as a calibration check rather than as primary validation.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ground-truth permutation analysis</span> establishes that permutation-induced dispersion precisely follows <math id="S1.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\log n)</annotation></semantics></math> across models. <span id="S1.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Causal dose-response studies</span> establish that information content, not just prompt length, determines hallucination rates. <span id="S1.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pre-specified permutation audits</span> on 528 held-out QA tasks prevent post-hoc selection bias.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S1.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S1.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our work synthesizes multiple research streams. While <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al. [2022]</a></cite> established Bayesian interpretations, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Falck et al. [2024]</a></cite> documented permutation invariance violations, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Farquhar et al. [2024]</a></cite> developed detection methods, no prior work explained how these phenomena coexist or provided predictive frameworks. By showing positional processing creates an inherent gap between average-case and worst-case behavior through a positional Jensen inequality, we provide the missing theoretical foundation. Rather than treating hallucinations as inevitable <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kalai and Vempala [2024]</a></cite> or relying on post-hoc detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Farquhar et al. [2024]</a></cite>, practitioners can now predict and prevent failures through principled information management.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+</section>
+<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>
+
+<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bayesian interpretations, MDL, and positional encodings.</span> A large body of work ties transformers to Bayesian inference: in-context learning as implicit Bayes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al. [2022]</a></cite>, approximate Bayesian model averaging <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. [2023]</a></cite>, near-optimal predictive power <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al. [2023]</a></cite>, and full Bayesian inference comparable to MCMC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Reuter et al. [2024]</a></cite>. However, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Falck et al. [2024]</a></cite> show that LLMs violate permutation invariance. The compression-learning connection has deep roots in Minimum Description Length (MDL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grünwald [2007]</a></cite>, with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Delétang et al. [2023]</a></cite> establishing equivalence between language modeling and compression. Positional encodings fundamentally alter behavior. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. [2024]</a></cite> documented systematic “lost-in-the-middle” effects. Our <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\log n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\log n)</annotation></semantics></math> bounds with explicit constants provide finer characterization connecting to compression failure.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hallucination detection vs prevention.</span>  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Farquhar et al. [2024]</a></cite> introduced semantic entropy for detection, achieving AUROC 0.790 by clustering semantically equivalent responses. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kalai and Vempala [2024]</a></cite> proved calibrated models must hallucinate at rates approximated by Good-Turing estimation. Multiple 2024 papers adopted “LLMs as lossy compression” perspectives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al. [2024]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vasilatos et al. [2024]</a></cite>, but without formal frameworks. While these works provide detection methods or prove inevitability, our EDFL offers the first predictive theory linking compression failure to hallucination with preventive measures through information budgeting.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Theory: Order-Sensitive Information-Theoretic Guarantees</h2>
+
+<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formalize how positional processing creates systematic deviations from Bayesian behavior while maintaining average-case optimality.</p>
+</div>
+<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Setup and Notation</h3>
+
+<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})</annotation></semantics></math> be a sequence with sufficient statistic <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T(X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T(X)</annotation></semantics></math> for predicting target <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> denote a permutation of chunk indices <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{1,\ldots,n\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,\ldots,n\}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math> a content-preserving reordering map where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Gamma_{\pi}(X)=(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(n)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Gamma_{\pi}(X)=(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(n)})</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="S_{\pi}(\cdot)=\Pr(\cdot|\Gamma_{\pi}(X))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>Pr</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\pi}(\cdot)=\Pr(\cdot|\Gamma_{\pi}(X))</annotation></semantics></math> the model’s predictive distribution given permuted input. Define <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\pi}(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1})|\Gamma_{\pi}(x)]" display="inline" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\pi}(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1})|\Gamma_{\pi}(x)]</annotation></semantics></math> as the prediction under permutation <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{q}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[q_{\pi}(x)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>q</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{q}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[q_{\pi}(x)]</annotation></semantics></math> as the average prediction over permutations. All expectations over <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> are conditional on fixed item <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. We assume <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\ll S_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>≪</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>π</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\ll S_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> (absolute continuity), smoothing zero-probability tokens with <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon=10^{-9}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon=10^{-9}</annotation></semantics></math> in practice. We write <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\text{pair}}:=\mathbb{E}_{\pi,\pi^{\prime}}|q_{\pi}(x)-q_{\pi^{\prime}}(x)|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>pair</mtext></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\text{pair}}:=\mathbb{E}_{\pi,\pi^{\prime}}|q_{\pi}(x)-q_{\pi^{\prime}}(x)|</annotation></semantics></math> for the expected pairwise absolute difference across independent permutations.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All information quantities (KL divergences, information budgets, Jensen gaps) are reported in nats unless otherwise noted.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Quantified Martingale Violations</h3>
+
+<div id="Thmdefinition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
+<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmdefinition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 1</span></span><span id="Thmdefinition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Permutation-induced residual)<span id="Thmdefinition1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
+<div id="Thmdefinition1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="Thmdefinition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmdefinition1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For the Answer/Refusal indicator <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> and position-aware predictions <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\pi}(x):=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1})|\Gamma_{\pi}(x)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\pi}(x):=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{n+1})|\Gamma_{\pi}(x)]</annotation></semantics></math>, the permutation residual is <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\pi}(x):=q_{\pi}(x)-\bar{q}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>q</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\pi}(x):=q_{\pi}(x)-\bar{q}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{q}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[q_{\pi}(x)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>q</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{q}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[q_{\pi}(x)]</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
+</div>
+</div>
+<div id="Thmassumption1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
