+<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Evaluation</h2>
+
+<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Settings</h3>
+
+<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
+<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.1 </span>Dataset</h4>
+
+<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To verify the effectiveness of <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Patient-Zero</span> in constructing and simulating patients, we followed existing research practices <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2024a)</a></cite> by randomly selecting six medical departments with common diseases from a department and disease list. Finally, the following medical departments are adopted: Psychiatry, Urology, Orthopedics, Ophthalmology, Endocrinology, and General Surgery, and for each department we generated 10,000 synthetic patient records. The knowledge base used to generate the patient records is derived from the Baidu Health Encyclopedia<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
+                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
+                
+                
+                
+              <a href="https://jiankang.baidu.com/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://jiankang.baidu.com/</a></span></span></span>.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the selected diseases, demographic data including gender and age, were estimated based on typical medical practices. Gender was evenly distributed for general conditions, while gender-specific conditions were assigned accordingly. Age was categorized into three groups: children (0-17), adults (18-59), and elderly (60-85), covering a broad range of medical concerns.
+Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Synthetic Patient Record ‣ Patient-Zero: A Unified Framework for Real-Record-Free Patient Agent Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> shows an example of the generated record.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
+<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.2 </span>Evaluation Metrics</h4>
+
+<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The quality of synthetic medical records is typically assessed through quantitative metrics to ensure the generated data are accurate and sufficiently diverse, so <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">accuracy</span> and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">diversity</span> related metrics are adopted: 1)
+Accuracy is formulated as the ratio of the number of patient records that are precisely aligned with medical standards to the total number of patient records, which is calculated by
+Hippomistral-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Acikgoz et al. (2024)</a></cite> with CoT in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.1.3 Baselines and Implementation Details ‣ 4.1 Experimental Settings ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Patient-Zero: A Unified Framework for Real-Record-Free Patient Agent Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
+2) Diversity is evaluated using metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE-L, and Cosine Similarity with default parameters.
+We use BERTScore <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2020)</a></cite> and GPTScore <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al. (2024)</a></cite> to measure the semantic similarity of synthetic patient record datatext <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al. (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the conversation ability of the generated patient agents, we focus on three core dimensions:
+<span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dialogue consistency</span> measures the extent to which the patient agent’s responses align with the generated patient record. <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Emotional consistency</span> and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">conversational fluency</span> are each rated on a 7-point scale by GPT-4o. The former metric evaluates the consistency of emotional expressions to the predefined patient features, while the latter assesses the naturalness and fluidity of the language used.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S4.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
+<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.3 </span>Baselines and Implementation Details</h4>
+
+<div id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare our <span id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Patient-Zero</span> framework with existing baselines that generate synthetic patient records using real medical data.
+LDP-GAN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gwon et al. (2024)</a></cite> generates synthetic patient medical records by using GANs and local differential privacy (LDP), adding noise to the synthetic data to protect individual privacy.
+Synthea <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Walonoski et al. (2017)</a></cite> simulates realistic medical histories and health records using publicly available health statistics and clinical guidelines.
+The Avatar method <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guillaudeux et al. (2023)</a></cite> generates synthetic data by using a patient-centered approach to create a local random simulation for each original observation.</p>
+</div>
+<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
+<div id="S4.T1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:73.2pt;vertical-align:-33.6pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(28.2pt,-6.0pt) scale(1.1955269894742,1.1955269894742) ;">

+<div id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To verify the flexibility of our <span id="S4.SS1.SSS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Patient-Zero</span>, we use four distinct LLMs, namely Doubao (Doubao-pro-32k), GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-1106), GPT-4o-mini (gpt-4o-mini), and GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06), to generate medical records in all experiments. The temperature is set to 1.0, with maximum tokens of 4,096 to limit response length.</p>

+</section>

+<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">

(2024)</a></cite> and Llama3-OpenBioLLM-8B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ankit Pal (2024)</a></cite>.</p>

+<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Performance of Generated Records ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Patient-Zero: A Unified Framework for Real-Record-Free Patient Agent Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the impact of direct generation versus our multi-step generation strategies, with and without outlines, across different LLM backbones.
+Patient-Zero consistently outperforms other approaches, achieving the highest accuracy and the lowest similarity scores.
+The capability of the model matters, as different LLMs exhibit varying performance gains from multi-step refinement.
+Multi-step generation without outline (Patient-Zero <sub id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_sub">w/o outline</sub>) underperforms compared to the outlined version across all metrics, highlighting the importance of explicit hierarchical structuring for coherent clinical data synthesis.
+Direct generation struggles with diversity, indicating a tendency towards verbatim replication.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Performance of Patient Agent Interaction</h3>
+
+<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this experiment, we randomly selected 10 generated patients from each department for evaluation (60 patients in total). Each patient participated in two types of dialogue sessions: cross-dialogue and single dialogue. In the cross-dialogue setting, each patient underwent two rounds of dialogue, with a total of 13 questions asked per round by a doctor agent, totalling 1,560 dialogues. The single dialogue setting involved only one round of conversation per patient, totalling 780 dialogues.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We compared different input formats, including structured JSON (for hierarchical data), unstructured text (mimicking clinical notes) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Irugalbandara (2024)</a></cite>, with our atomic patient agent memory to evaluate the quality of patient agent interaction.</p>
+</div>

Our structured memory architecture significantly improves over the baselines, enhancing the alignment of patient responses and emotions with their records and predefined styles. It also generates more coherent and natural responses, improving overall interaction quality. Notably, incorporating memory updates in cross-dialogue interactions leads to a significant improvement in performance, strengthening role-playing capabilities.</p>

+<td id="S4.T5.2.1.6.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.T5.2.1.6.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">91.67</span></td></tr>
+<tr id="S4.T5.2.1.7" class="ltx_tr">
+<td id="S4.T5.2.1.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">General Surgery</td>
+<td id="S4.T5.2.1.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">84.00</td>
+<td id="S4.T5.2.1.7.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T5.2.1.7.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">90.00</span></td>
+<td id="S4.T5.2.1.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T5.2.1.7.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">90.00</span></td></tr>
+</table>
+</span></div>
+<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Performance comparison across six medical departments in MedQA. The table presents accuracy scores for different methods in different departments.</figcaption>
+</figure>
+<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To validate the effectiveness of our synthetic medical records on external tasks, we adopted the medical record utilization approach from existing research work  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2024a)</a></cite>. We incorporated the generated records into the training process of doctor agents and ultimately evaluated the agents’ performance on the MedQA dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al. (2021)</a></cite> with corresponding clinical departments.
+We use GPT-4o as the backbone model due to its prior performance in previous experiments. GPT-4o without training and GPT-4o with direct synthetic medical records are taken as baselines.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Following the experimental setup in the aforementioned paper, we tested the models on the corresponding MedQA subset.
+Experimental results in Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.4 External Evaluation ‣ 4 Evaluation ‣ Patient-Zero: A Unified Framework for Real-Record-Free Patient Agent Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> show that training with high-quality virtual patient data from our <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Patient-Zero</span> allows the Doctor Agent to outperform both the baseline and direct augmentation methods across all medical specialties, enhancing its ability to handle medical complexities. GPT-4o baseline evaluation on the MedQA benchmark reveals its limitations, with the lowest accuracy across specialties.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
+<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Case Study: Human Expert Evaluation</h3>
+
+<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the clinical realism of our synthetic patient data, we conducted human annotation to verify the quality of the generated medical cases. Physicians at a Class III (tertiary-level) hospital in Beijing China, which works in General Surgery department, to review a randomly selected subset of the synthetic patient records. The feedback from the human experts indicated that the synthetic patient records largely met expectations for clinical realism.
+However, they observed that some records occasionally lacked minor but important elements of a comprehensive clinical evaluation, such as detailed physical examination findings and conclusions.
+This feedback is valuable for future refinements of our framework to enhance the depth of clinical detail in the synthetic data.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+</section>
+<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion and Future Work</h2>
+
+<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our study presents a multi-step generation framework that systematically enhances synthetic patient records through three core innovations: 1) a multi-step outline generation process guided by medical guidelines, 2) a real-time triplet evaluation mechanism with a memory update process for consistency checks, and 3) an adaptive conversational agent design supporting diverse interaction styles. Evaluations across medical specialties demonstrate measurable improvements in data accuracy, diversity, and MedQA accuracy compared to baseline methods. The system’s capacity to simulate context-aware dialogues provides new potentials for the usage of synthetic data in medical AI tasks.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our future research will focus on the integration of multimodal data to enable comprehensive medical record generation. Optimizing distribution-aware generation to help maintain statistical alignment between synthetic data and real-world distributions and demographic variations.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Limitations</h2>
+
+<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
+<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Clinical Validation Gap</h5>
+
+<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A limitation of this framework lies in its reliance on synthetic validation metrics rather than real-world clinical trials. While the system demonstrates improved MedQA accuracy and interaction plausibility in controlled evaluations, its performance remains unproven in organic healthcare settings. This raises concerns about external validity, particularly regarding the system’s ability to handle atypical symptom presentations, cultural communication differences, and complex medical complications that often challenge human clinicians.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
+<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Distribution Misalignment</h5>
+
+<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The generated data exhibits statistical deviations from real-world clinical distributions due to limitations in modeling regional epidemiological variations and disparities in healthcare access. The framework does not account for factors such as seasonal disease patterns and age-dependent clinical manifestations in disease prevalence and symptom presentation. These limitations may lead to an artificially homogenized synthetic patient cohort, potentially reducing the utility of the data for training models intended for deployment in diverse clinical environments.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
+<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Unable to Generate Multi-modal Patient Data</h5>
+
+<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Currently, our model can only generate textual features of patients, including imaging examination results, which are limited to textual conclusions without corresponding image content. Although these data can still be used for training doctor agents and other applications, they lack the completeness of real medical records. In the future, we plan to enhance and refine the relevant modules to improve the quality of synthetic patient data.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+</section>

+<section id="Ax1" class="ltx_appendix">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix">Appendix</h2>
+
+</section>
+<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Patient Case Studies</h2>
+
+<figure id="A1.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2509.11078v1/data_comparison.svg" id="A1.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/268;" width="476" height="268"></object>
+<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Comparison of direct generation and multi-step generation approaches for Sciatica patient cases. The direct generation method yields basic, less detailed cases, whereas the multi-step approach progressively refines details, enhancing granularity and realism.</figcaption>
+</figure>
+<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Appendix A Patient Case Studies ‣ Patient-Zero: A Unified Framework for Real-Record-Free Patient Agent Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, the direct generation method generates basic case patient records but lacks depth and precision. Symptoms like "pain, tingling, numbness, and difficulty walking" are noted without specifying location, severity, or triggers. Duration is limited to "4 weeks", with no mention of fluctuation or aggravating factors. Epidemiological data is superficial; a "sedentary lifestyle due to a desk job" offers no meaningful insight, while family history is erroneously marked as "None", ignoring hereditary factors. Examination results contain incorrect information, such as a "positive straight leg raising test at 60 degrees" (a value inconsistent with standard nerve tension tests), and imaging findings vaguely mention "compression at L4-L5 vertebrae" without detailing structural abnormalities or nerve involvement.</p>
+</div>
+<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Symptoms are described comprehensively using the multi-step method, alongside contextual details like fluctuating intensity and responses to stretching. Epidemiological data incorporates a history of lumbar disc herniation, occasional exercise habits, and a BMI of 29, highlighting lifestyle and genetic risk factors. Family history correctly identifies a father with chronic back problems and a maternal uncle with herniated discs, offering valuable hereditary context. Examination findings are accurate and clinically relevant: a "positive straight leg raising test at 45 degrees" aligns with severe nerve root tension, while imaging identifies a "moderate protrusion of the L4-L5 disc compressing the left L5 nerve root". Electrophysiology confirms "denervation in muscles innervated by the L5 root", ruling out significant long-term damage.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Synthetic Patient Record</h2>
+
+<figure id="A2.F5" class="ltx_figure"><span id="A2.F5.2" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle">
+<span id="A2.F5.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<span id="A2.F5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">Basic Information</span></span>
+</span>
+<span id="A2.F5.p2" class="ltx_para">
+<span id="A2.F5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ID:</span> 10024
+<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.F5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Name:</span> Clara Gutierrez
+<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.F5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Gender:</span> Female
+<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.F5.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Age:</span> 47
+<br class="ltx_break"></span>
+</span>
+<span id="A2.F5.p3" class="ltx_para">
+<span id="A2.F5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">Epidemiology</span></span>
+</span>
+<span id="A2.F5.p4" class="ltx_para">
+<span id="A2.F5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Medical History:</span> Chronic pancreatitis diagnosed 5 years ago, history of gallstones, high cholesterol
+<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.F5.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lifestyle Factor:</span> Moderate alcohol consumption (social drinker), high-fat diet, sedentary lifestyle, former smoker (quit 2 years ago)
+<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.F5.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vaccination History:</span> Not vaccinated for hepatitis A or B
+<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.F5.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Family History:</span> Mother had gallbladder issues, father had pancreatitis and diabetes
+<br class="ltx_break"></span>
+</span>
+<span id="A2.F5.p5" class="ltx_para">
+<span id="A2.F5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">Disease Information</span></span>
+</span>
+<span id="A2.F5.p6" class="ltx_para">
+<span id="A2.F5.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F5.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Disease:</span> Pancreatitis
+<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.F5.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Level:</span> Severe
+<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.F5.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Symptoms:</span> Acute abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, dyspnea, hypotension, upper abdominal distension, elevated blood sugar
+<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.F5.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Duration:</span> Symptoms have been present for the last 10 days, worsening over the past 48 hours, with severe abdominal pain radiating to the back.
+<br class="ltx_break"></span>
+</span>
+<span id="A2.F5.p7" class="ltx_para">
+<span id="A2.F5.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.F5.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">Examination Results</span></span>
+<span id="A2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
+<span id="A2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
+<span id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<span id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Routine Blood Test:</span> Serum amylase level is significantly elevated at 450 U/L (normal range: 30-110 U/L) and lipase at 900 U/L (normal range: 0-160 U/L). Blood glucose is also elevated at 220 mg/dL, indicating possible pancreatic damage affecting insulin secretion.</span>
+</span></span>
+<span id="A2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
+<span id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<span id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Biochemical Test:</span> The white blood cell count is elevated at 14,000 cells/mm0̆0b3, suggesting an inflammatory response. Liver function tests show mild elevation in ALT at 60 U/L (normal range: 7-56 U/L) and alkaline phosphatase at 150 U/L (normal range: 44-147 U/L), indicating possible biliary involvement. Kidney function tests remain within normal limits.</span>
+</span></span>
+<span id="A2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
+<span id="A2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<span id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Imaging Tests:</span> CT scan of the abdomen reveals significant pancreatic edema with peritoneal fluid collection and a 3 cm pseåudocyst formation adjacent to the pancreas. No evidence of necrosis is noted. An abdominal ultrasound confirms the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder, with a dilated common bile duct measuring 10 mm.</span>
+</span></span>
+</span>
+</span></span>
+<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>A synthetic patient medical record generated for a severe Pancreatitis case.</figcaption>
+</figure>
+<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This case in Figure <a href="#A2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Appendix B Synthetic Patient Record ‣ Patient-Zero: A Unified Framework for Real-Record-Free Patient Agent Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> presents a patient with severe acute pancreatitis and multiple risk factors. The patient has a complex medical history, including chronic pancreatitis, gallstones, and hypercholesterolemia, compounded by an unhealthy lifestyle (high-fat diet and alcohol consumption). Imaging reveals pancreatic edema with pseudocyst formation and biliary abnormalities (gallstones with common bile duct dilation), suggesting biliary pancreatitis. Laboratory findings indicate significantly elevated pancreatic enzyme levels, inflammatory response, and glucose metabolism disorders, consistent with pancreatic parenchymal injury. A family history of pancreatic diseases and metabolic disorders warrants attention, while the lack of hepatitis vaccination may increase the risk of secondary infections. The disease course shows acute exacerbation, necessitating vigilance for potential progression from local complications to systemic multi-organ dysfunction.</p>
+</div>
+</section>
+<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
+<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Conversation</h2>
+
+<figure id="A3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2509.11078v1/doctor_patient_conversation.png" id="A3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/357;" width="476" height="357" alt="Refer to caption">
+<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Example of a patient agent conversational interaction where the patient has Social Anxiety Disorder. The dialogue demonstrates the patient’s responses to the doctor’s questions about age, allergies, relationship status, chronic illnesses, daily life challenges, and environmental factors. The interaction highlights the patient’s struggles with anxiety, depression, and social functioning, providing a realistic and empathetic representation of their condition.</figcaption>
+</figure>
+<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
+<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned in Figure <a href="#A3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Appendix C Conversation ‣ Patient-Zero: A Unified Framework for Real-Record-Free Patient Agent Generation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, a 24-year-old patient with Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) and comorbid depressive symptoms has experienced persistent anxiety since age 22, leading to severe social withdrawal and functional impairment. The patient exhibits cognitive distortions (fear of judgment) and behavioral avoidance, reinforcing isolation and distress. Daily activities, including work and errands, are disrupted, with crowded environments exacerbating symptoms. The presence of recurrent depressive episodes suggests potential Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) or anxiety-induced depression, requiring further assessment. Key risk factors include lack of social support and chronic avoidance. The doctor’s empathetic approach highlights the need for a structured treatment plan, such as CBT, SSRIs, and social skills training, to address both anxiety and depression while promoting gradual social reintegration.</p>
+</div>

However, the mechanisms of memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs remain poorly understood. In this paper, we propose the function token hypothesis to explain the workings of LLMs: During inference, function tokens activate the most predictive features from context and govern next token prediction (memory retrieval). During pre-training, predicting the next tokens (usually content tokens) that follow function tokens increases the number of learned features of LLMs and updates the model parameters (memory consolidation). Function tokens here roughly correspond to function words in linguistics, including punctuation marks, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions, in contrast to content tokens. Widening models yields diminishing returns, and extending context length does not improve fundamental expressivity. In contrast, depth scaling offers theoretically superior expressivity, yet current Transformer architectures struggle to train reliably at extreme depths. We revisit the Post-LayerNorm (Post-LN) formulation, whose instability at scale caused its replacement by Pre-LN in modern LLMs. We show that the central failure mode of Post-LN arises from the ResNet-style residual pathway, which introduces gradient vanishing in deep networks. +<article class="post-content">
+  <h1>ToMA: Token Merge with Attention for Diffusion Models</h1><span class="authors">Wenbo Lu,&nbsp;Shaoyi Zheng,&nbsp;Yuxuan Xia,&nbsp;Shengjie Wang</span>
+<div id="info"><i>Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning</i>,&nbsp;PMLR 267:40930-40951,&nbsp;2025.
+  </div> <!-- info -->
+  
+  <h4>Abstract</h4>
+  <div id="abstract" class="abstract">
+    Diffusion models excel in high-fidelity image generation but face scalability limits due to transformers’ quadratic attention complexity. Plug-and-play token reduction methods like ToMeSD and ToFu reduce FLOPs by merging redundant tokens in generated images but rely on GPU-inefficient operations (e.g., sorting, scattered writes), introducing overheads that negate theoretical speedups when paired with optimized attention implementations (e.g., FlashAttention). To bridge this gap, we propose <b>To</b>ken <b>M</b>erge with <b>A</b>ttention (ToMA), an off-the-shelf method that redesigns token reduction for GPU-aligned efficiency, with three key contributions: 1) a reformulation of token merging as a submodular optimization problem to select diverse tokens; 2) merge/unmerge as an attention-like linear transformation via GPU-friendly matrix operations; and 3) exploiting latent locality and sequential redundancy (pattern reuse) to minimize overhead. ToMA reduces SDXL/Flux generation latency by 24%/23% (DINO $\Delta <$ 0.07), outperforming prior methods. This work bridges the gap between theoretical and practical efficiency for transformers in diffusion.
+  </div>

+%E Aarti Singh
+%E Maryam Fazel
+%E Daniel Hsu
+%E Simon Lacoste-Julien
+%E Felix Berkenkamp
+%E Tegan Maharaj
+%E Kiri Wagstaff
+%E Jerry Zhu	
+%F pmlr-v267-lu25v
+%I PMLR
+%P 40930--40951
+%U https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/lu25v.html
+%V 267
+%X Diffusion models excel in high-fidelity image generation but face scalability limits due to transformers’ quadratic attention complexity. Plug-and-play token reduction methods like ToMeSD and ToFu reduce FLOPs by merging redundant tokens in generated images but rely on GPU-inefficient operations (e.g., sorting, scattered writes), introducing overheads that negate theoretical speedups when paired with optimized attention implementations (e.g., FlashAttention). To bridge this gap, we propose <b>To</b>ken <b>M</b>erge with <b>A</b>ttention (ToMA), an off-the-shelf method that redesigns token reduction for GPU-aligned efficiency, with three key contributions: 1) a reformulation of token merging as a submodular optimization problem to select diverse tokens; 2) merge/unmerge as an attention-like linear transformation via GPU-friendly matrix operations; and 3) exploiting latent locality and sequential redundancy (pattern reuse) to minimize overhead. ToMA reduces SDXL/Flux generation latency by 24%/23% (DINO $\Delta <$ 0.07), outperforming prior methods. This work bridges the gap between theoretical and practical efficiency for transformers in diffusion.
+</code>

+"""Read captured source HTML as a small tree; no network or report writes."""
+from html.parser import HTMLParser
+import json
+import re
+from SUP_inspect_20261012 import read
+
+
+class Node:
+    def __init__(self, tag, attrs=(), parent=None):
+        self.tag, self.attrs, self.parent = tag, dict(attrs), parent
+        self.children = []
+
+    def text(self):
+        return " ".join(" ".join(x if isinstance(x, str) else x.text()
+                                 for x in self.children).split())
+
+    def all(self, tag=None):
+        for child in self.children:
+            if isinstance(child, Node):
+                if tag is None or child.tag == tag:
+                    yield child
+                yield from child.all(tag)
+
+
+class Tree(HTMLParser):
+    VOID = set("area base br col embed hr img input link meta param source track wbr".split())
+
+    def __init__(self, source):
+        super().__init__()
+        self.root = self.current = Node("root")
+        self.feed(source)
+
+    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
+        node = Node(tag, attrs, self.current)
+        self.current.children.append(node)
+        if tag not in self.VOID:
+            self.current = node
+
+    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
+        node = self.current
+        while node.parent and node.tag != tag:
+            node = node.parent
+        if node.tag == tag:
+            self.current = node.parent
+
+    def handle_data(self, text):
+        self.current.children.append(text)
+
+
+def next_data(name):
+    chunks = []
+    for script in Tree(read(name)).root.all("script"):
+        text = script.text()
+        match = re.fullmatch(r"self\.__next_f\.push\((\[.*\])\)", text)
+        if match:
+            value = json.loads(match.group(1))
+            if len(value) == 2 and isinstance(value[1], str):
+                chunks.append(value[1])
+    return "".join(chunks)
+
+
+def objects(text):
+    decoder = json.JSONDecoder()
+    for match in re.finditer(r"\{", text):
+        try:
+            value, _ = decoder.raw_decode(text, match.start())
+            yield value
+        except ValueError:
+            pass
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    import sys
+    root = Tree(read(sys.argv[1])).root
+    mode = sys.argv[2]
+    if mode == "times":
+        for node in root.all("time"):
+            print(node.attrs, node.parent.text()[:600])
+    elif mode == "links":
+        for node in root.all("a"):
+            print(node.attrs.get("href"), node.text())
+    elif mode == "cards":
+        for node in root.all():
+            if node.tag in ("article", "h2", "h3"):
+                print(node.tag, node.attrs, node.parent.text()[:800])
+    elif mode == "tables":
+        for node in root.all("table"):
+            print(node.attrs, node.text())

+# New Released
+
+> Follow along with updates across Z.AI’s models
+
+## Models
+
+<Update label="2026-08-26" description="  GLM-5.3-Flash">
+  * Native visual capabilities enable the model to observe interfaces, rendering results, and interaction feedback—creating a closed loop across code, browsers, and GUIs.
+
+  * Efficient hybrid architecture: Combines linear and sparse attention with 320B total parameters and 18B activated, significantly reducing compute and KV-cache requirements.
+
+  * Beyond coding: Supports office document and financial research workflows, autonomously breaking down goals, using tools, and refining outputs. Learn more in our [documentation](/guides/vlm/glm-5.3-flash).\*
+</Update>
+
+<Update label="2026-08-18" description="  GLM-5.3">
+  * Stronger Coding Capabilities: GLM-5.3 delivers a significant improvement in coding capabilities, achieving a 50% gain over GLM-5.2 on Z.ai Code Bench and reaching state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance among open-source models on public benchmarks, including Terminal Bench 3.0.
+
+  * Emergent Cybersecurity Capabilities: GLM-5.3 matches Mythos 5 in white-box code review and vulnerability discovery. In collaboration with multiple cybersecurity teams, it has been tested on real-world targets and has identified a total of 2,436 vulnerabilities, including 1,097 medium- and high-severity vulnerabilities.Learn more in our [documentation](https://docs.z.ai/guides/llm/glm-5.3).\*
+</Update>
+
+<Update label="2026-06-16" description="  GLM-5.2">
+  * Supports 1M lossless context, significantly improving long-horizon task capabilities and reducing context drift and goal forgetting in complex tasks
+
+  * Achieves open-source SOTA performance on coding and long-horizon task benchmarks, delivering more stable results in complex system engineering and deep debugging
+
+  * Significantly improves the real-world developer experience, with more reliable project-level context handling, adherence to engineering standards, and multi-platform development. Learn more in our [documentation](/guides/llm/glm-5.2).\*
+</Update>
+
+<Update label="2026-04-07" description="  GLM-5.1">
+  * Designed for long-horizon tasks, GLM-5.1 can work independently for up to 8 hours in a single run, enabling a full loop from planning and execution to iterative refinement and final delivery.
+
+  * It demonstrates stronger engineering intelligence across autonomous planning, sustained execution, bug fixing, and strategy iteration, while achieving comprehensive capability alignment with Claude Opus 4.6. Built with multi-turn SFT, RL, and a process-quality evaluation framework, GLM-5.1 further improves stability, consistency, and tool use over extended tasks. Learn more in our [documentation](/guides/llm/glm-5.1).\*
+</Update>
+
+<Update label="2026-02-12" description="  GLM-5">
+  * Designed for complex system engineering and long-range Agent tasks, GLM-5 shifts the paradigm from coding to engineering, demonstrating strong deep-reasoning performance in backend architecture, complex algorithms, and stubborn bug fixing.
+
+  * It directly benchmarks against Claude Opus 4.5 in code-logic density and systems-engineering capability, and integrates DeepSeek Sparse Attention for higher token efficiency while preserving long-context quality.Learn more in our [documentation](/guides/llm/glm-5).\*
+</Update>
+
+<Update label="2026-01-14" description="  GLM-Image">
+  * We’ve launched GLM-Image, a state-of-the-art image generation model built on a multimodal architecture and fully trained on domestic chips, combining autoregressive semantic understanding with diffusion-based decoding to deliver high-quality, controllable visual generation.
+  * The update significantly enhances performance in knowledge-intensive scenarios, with more stable and accurate text rendering inside images, making GLM-Image especially well suited for commercial design, educational illustrations, and content-rich visual applications.Learn more in our [documentation](/guides/image/glm-image).\*
+</Update>
+
+<Update label="2025-12-22" description="  GLM-4.7">
+  * We’ve released GLM-4.7, our foundation model with significant improvements in coding, reasoning, and agentic capabilities. It delivers more reliable code generation, stronger long-context understanding, and improved end-to-end task execution across real-world development workflows.
+  * The update brings open-source SOTA performance on major coding and reasoning benchmarks, enhanced agentic coding for goal-driven, multi-step tasks, and improved front-end and document generation quality. Learn more in our [documentation](/guides/llm/glm-4.7).\*
+</Update>
+
+<Update label="2025-09-30" description="  GLM-4.6">
+  * We’ve launched GLM-4.6, the flagship coding model, showcasing enhanced performance in both public benchmarks and real-world programming tasks, making it the leading coding model in China.
+  * The update also expands the context window to 200K, improving its ability to handle longer code and complex agent tasks. Learn more in our [documentation](/guides/llm/glm-4.6).\*
